Interpret the confidence level correctly
Shark Tank data The parameter is fixed. The endpoints of the interval vary from sample to sample. The confidence level \(1-\alpha\) describes the procedure. If we repeat the same valid procedure on many random samples, a fraction \(1-\alpha\) of the resulting intervals contains the parameter. For a 95% level, that is about 95 intervals in 100. For a 90% level, the intervals are narrower and about 90 in 100 contain the parameter.
The simulation in Figure 9.3 repeats the random sample and the calculation of a 95% interval 100 times. The fixed target is the mean equity offered (equity_offered_pct) among all 1,441 recorded pitches, 13.21%. It is known here because the file is the whole population.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(209)
B_coverage <- 100
n_coverage <- 100
target_mean <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)
ci_lower <- ci_upper <- ci_centre <- numeric(B_coverage)

for (i in seq_len(B_coverage)) {
  repeated_sample <- sample(
    sharks$equity_offered_pct,
    size = n_coverage,
    replace = FALSE
  )
  repeated_mean <- mean(repeated_sample)
  repeated_se <- sd(repeated_sample) / sqrt(n_coverage)
  repeated_critical <- qt(0.975, df = n_coverage - 1)
  ci_centre[i] <- repeated_mean
  ci_lower[i] <- repeated_mean - repeated_critical * repeated_se
  ci_upper[i] <- repeated_mean + repeated_critical * repeated_se
}

intervals <- data.frame(
  lower = ci_lower, centre = ci_centre, upper = ci_upper,
  covers = ifelse(ci_lower <= target_mean & ci_upper >= target_mean,
                  "contains the target mean", "misses the target mean")
)
intervals <- intervals[order(intervals$centre), ]
intervals$position <- seq_len(B_coverage)

ggplot(intervals, aes(y = position, colour = covers)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = position),
               linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(x = centre), size = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = target_mean, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#C98B2E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = target_mean, y = B_coverage + 3.5,
           label = "mu == 13.21", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("contains the target mean" = "#009E73",
                                 "misses the target mean" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Mean equity offered (%)",
       y = "Repeated sample (ordered by estimate)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )








Figure 9.3: One hundred repetitions of the same procedure: draw 100 random pitches, compute a 95% t interval for the mean equity offered. Green intervals contain the fixed target mean (gold dashed line). Orange intervals miss it. In this run, 96 of 100 intervals cover the target.





Each horizontal segment in Figure 9.3 is one 95% confidence interval. Its dot is that sample’s mean. The gold dashed vertical line is the fixed target mean, 13.21. In this run (seed 209), 96 of 100 intervals cross the line. A new run does not have to give exactly 95, but across many repetitions the proportion approaches 95% when the conditions of the procedure hold.
The following sentence may look natural, but it is wrong:

“There is a 95% probability that the population mean is in my interval.”

Before the sample is drawn, the endpoints of the interval are random, and the 95% applies to them. After the sample is drawn, the interval \((11.23, 14.29)\) consists of two fixed numbers. It either contains the fixed parameter or it does not. Nothing random is left, so the probability of 95% no longer applies. The correct sentence is:

“This interval was produced by a procedure that captures the fixed population mean in about 95% of repeated valid samples.”

The same holds for every other confidence level, with 90% or 99% in place of 95%.


How many customers must I ask?
A larger sample gives a smaller margin of error: four times the observations halve it. A founder often asks a more direct question before a survey: how large must the sample be to reach a given precision?
The answer comes from the formula for the margin of error, used the other way round. Before the survey there is no sample, so there is no \(s\). So for planning you use a value for \(\sigma\) from a pilot survey (a small test survey) or from an earlier study. This value is called a planning value, and you treat it as known. That is why the formula uses a z value: \(m=z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n\). Choose the largest margin of error you accept and call it \(m\). Then solve for \(n\):
\[
z_{1-\alpha/2}\times\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\le m
\qquad\text{gives}\qquad
n\ge\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\times\sigma}{m}\right)^2.
\]
For a 95% confidence level, \(z_{0.975}=1.96\) and the formula is \(n\ge(1.96\times\sigma/m)^2\). For 90% use \(z_{0.95}=1.645\), and for 99% use \(z_{0.995}=2.576\). Always round the result up to the next whole number.

Example 9.2 (Worked example: a sample size for a margin of 2 euros) An invented example. You want to know the average order value of your customers to within 2 euros, at the 95% confidence level. How many customers must you survey?

Planning value. The formula needs \(\sigma\), which you do not know before the survey. A small pilot survey gave an SD of about 12 euros, so use \(\sigma=12\) as a planning value. The target margin of 2 euros is one sixth of that SD.
Sample size. We need
\[
n\ge\left(\frac{1.96\times 12}{2}\right)^2=11.76^2\approx 138.3.
\]
Round up. Survey \(n=139\) customers. Always round up: with 138 customers the margin would be slightly above 2 euros.

Halving the margin to 1 euro needs \((1.96\times 12/1)^2=23.52^2\approx 553.2\), so 554 customers. Half the margin costs about four times the sample, as the square-root rule of Lecture 8 says. A higher confidence level also needs more observations. A margin of 2 euros at the 99% level needs \((2.576\times 12/2)^2=15.456^2\approx 238.9\), so 239 customers.

n_needed <- c(margin_2_euros = (1.96 * sigma_plan / 2)^2,
              margin_1_euro  = (1.96 * sigma_plan / 1)^2,
              margin_2_euros_99_percent = (2.576 * sigma_plan / 2)^2)
n_needed

The same recipe for a proportion
Shark Tank data A proportion is the mean of a 0/1 variable (Lecture 8). Take the deal indicator (deal_on_show), which is 1 if a pitch ends in a deal and 0 if not. Let \(p\) be the proportion of all pitches that end in a deal. The sample proportion \(\widehat P\) is the sample mean of the indicators, so the results of Lecture 8 apply directly:
\[
E[\widehat P]=p,
\qquad
\operatorname{SD}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.
\]
There is no separate \(\sigma\) to know or to estimate. The spread of a 0/1 variable is determined by \(p\) itself, because \(\sigma^2=p(1-p)\) (Lecture 7). By the central limit theorem, if \(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10\) (Lecture 8),
\[
Z=\frac{\widehat P-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}
\]
is approximately standard normal. The steps of the mean case then give two bounds around \(\widehat P\). But these bounds contain \(p\) inside the square root, and \(p\) is the unknown parameter. The solution is the standard error of Lecture 8: replace \(p\) inside the square root by its estimator \(\widehat P\). For large \(n\) this changes little. The interval estimator is
\[
\widehat P\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat P(1-\widehat P)}{n}},
\]
and it captures \(p\) with a probability of approximately \(1-\alpha\). With the data put in, the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(p\) is
\[
\hat p\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}.
\]
It has the general form of every interval in this course. The estimate is \(\hat p\), the critical value is a z value, and the standard error is \(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\).






Optional: the bounds that still contain \(p\)





The same steps as for the mean, applied to \(Z=(\widehat P-p)/\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\), give with a probability of approximately \(1-\alpha\)
\[
\widehat P-z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}
\ \le\ p\ \le\
\widehat P+z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} .
\]
Here the mean and the proportion differ. These bounds contain \(p\), the unknown that they should capture, so they cannot be calculated. Replacing \(p\) inside the square root by the consistent estimator \(\widehat P\) turns the bounds into sample statistics:
\[
L=\widehat P-z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat P(1-\widehat P)}{n}},
\qquad
U=\widehat P+z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat P(1-\widehat P)}{n}} .
\]



Three remarks.

The critical value is a z value, not a t value. We used the t distribution for the mean because, in a normal population, there is an exact result for replacing \(\sigma\) by \(S\). No such result exists for a proportion. The interval is a large-sample approximation from the start, so \(z\) is the right critical value.
Check the condition with \(\hat p\). The success-failure rule contains the unknown \(p\). In practice, you check it with the sample proportion: \(n\hat p\ge10\) and \(n(1-\hat p)\ge10\).
The margin of error depends on \(\hat p\), which is not known before the sample is drawn. So this formula does not give a required sample size directly, unlike the mean case with a planning value for \(\sigma\).

Given values. The number of successes, \(n\), \(\hat p\), the confidence level, and the critical value \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) from the question or the formula sheet.

Interval. \((\hat p-\text{margin},\ \hat p+\text{margin})\).

Formula. \(\widehat P\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat P(1-\widehat P)/n}\). It may be used because \(n\hat p=64\) and \(n(1-\hat p)=36\) are both at least 10.
Given values. 64 deals in \(n=100\) pitches, so \(\hat p=0.64\). The confidence level is 95%, so the critical value is \(z_{0.975}=1.96\).

\[

Interval. The interval is
\[
(0.64-0.094,\ 0.64+0.094)=(0.546,\ 0.734).
\]
Conclusion. With 95% confidence, between about 55% and 73% of all recorded pitches end in a deal. The value 0.50 lies outside the interval. At the 5% level we can conclude that the deal proportion differs from one half, and the interval shows that it is higher.


Because the file is the whole population, we can check both intervals. The mean equity offered among all 1,441 recorded pitches is \(\mu=13.21\)%, inside \((11.23,\ 14.29)\). The deal proportion is \(p=0.612\), inside \((0.546,\ 0.734)\).

# Known only because the file is the whole population.
c(population_mean_equity = mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct),
  population_deal_proportion = mean(sharks$deal_on_show))

    population_mean_equity population_deal_proportion 
                13.2076128                  0.6120749 

range(sharks$equity_offered_pct)   # smallest and largest equity offered

[1]   1 100




From interval to test
Shark Tank data An interval answers one kind of question: which values of the parameter are compatible with the sample? A second kind of question works the other way round. Someone proposes one specific value, and the question is whether the sample is compatible with it. The advisor in the driving question says that pitches typically offer 15% equity. The sample of 100 pitches has a mean of 12.76. Is the advisor’s figure compatible with this sample, or does the sample show that the figure is wrong? Answering questions of this kind is called hypothesis testing. This section sets up the question. Lecture 10 answers it.

A test compares two hypotheses
A hypothesis test is a decision between two statements about an unknown population parameter, such as a mean \(\mu\) or a proportion \(p\). The decision is based on a random sample. The two statements cannot both be true.

Definition
Null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis. The null hypothesis \(H_0\) and the alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) are two statements about a parameter that cannot both be true. A hypothesis test uses a random sample to decide between them. The decision is either “reject \(H_0\)” or “do not reject \(H_0\)”.

You cannot choose freely which statement is the null and which is the alternative. The alternative is the claim that the researcher wants to establish (to show with data): the research question, the new finding. The null is its opposite: the default position, “there is no effect or difference”. Take a medical trial that hopes to show that a new drug changes blood pressure. It puts “the drug has an effect” in \(H_1\) and “the drug has no effect” in \(H_0\). The reason follows below.


The founder’s hypotheses
A founder believes that the advisor’s figure is wrong. Her claim is about the population mean \(\mu\) of the equity offered: \(\mu\ne15\). The hypotheses are \(H_0:\mu=15\) versus \(H_1:\mu\ne15\).


Two conclusions that are not symmetric
A test ends with one of two conclusions. They do not have the same strength.

Reject \(H_0\). The evidence in the data is strong enough to support \(H_1\). In the founder’s example: “we found enough evidence that the mean equity offered differs from 15%.” This conclusion can be wrong, but only with a small probability that is fixed in advance. Lecture 10 makes this precise. It is the strong conclusion.
Do not reject \(H_0\). The data did not give enough evidence against \(H_0\). This is not the same as concluding that \(H_0\) is true. In the example: “we do not have enough evidence that the mean equity offered differs from 15%, but we cannot claim that it equals 15%.” The sample may have been too small or too variable to answer the question. It is the weak conclusion.

The difference comes from what a test controls. A test is built so that the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) wrongly stays below a small number fixed in advance. The construction sets no limit on the other mistake: not rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false. So “reject” is a conclusion with a guarantee, and “do not reject” is a conclusion without one. This is also why we put the claim to be established in \(H_1\). If the founder’s claim were in \(H_0\), the best result for her would be “do not reject”, which establishes nothing.
A court works in the same way. The court starts from the assumption that the accused person is innocent (\(H_0\)). The prosecutor must prove guilt (\(H_1\)). The verdict is “guilty” or “not guilty”, never “innocent”. The system keeps the probability of finding an innocent person guilty small. In return, it accepts that a guilty person is sometimes found not guilty.


How a test differs from a confidence interval
The interval and the test use the same pieces: an estimate, a standard error, and a known distribution. But they ask different questions. The interval starts from the sample and returns a set of values for the parameter. Its guarantee is how often the method captures the true value. The test starts from one value proposed in advance and returns a decision about it. Its guarantee is how often the method rejects a value that is true. Lecture 10 shows that for a mean the interval and the two-sided test lead to the same decision.


The two-sided test used in this course
The founder’s claim has no direction: the advisor’s figure can be wrong in either direction. A test of such a claim is called a two-sided test. It is the standard choice, and the safer one. This course works with the two-sided test
\[
H_0:\mu=\mu_0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0 ,
\]
where \(\mu_0\) is a fixed, known number: the value that is tested. An optional box in Lecture 10 describes tests with a direction, called one-sided tests. For the advisor’s claim, \(\mu_0=15\):
\[
H_0:\mu=15
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\mu\ne15 .
\]
State both hypotheses from the question, before you look at the sample.


The test statistic
As for the interval, the first step is the case with \(\sigma\) known. The setting is the same: a population with unknown mean \(\mu\) and known SD \(\sigma\), a random sample \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), and a population that is normal or an \(n\) that is large. For the Shark Tank file we can calculate this case with real numbers, because \(\sigma=8.44\) is known.
The obvious evidence against \(H_0\) is the distance between the sample mean and the tested value, \(\bar x-\mu_0\). For the advisor’s claim it is \(12.76-15=-2.24\) percentage points. A distance alone is hard to judge. A difference of 2.24 points is large if sample means rarely lie more than one point from \(\mu\). It is small if they often lie five points away. The right scale is the standard deviation of the sample mean, \(\sigma/\sqrt n\). Dividing by it gives the test statistic
\[
Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}.
\]
This is the standardised sample mean of the interval section, with \(\mu_0\) in place of \(\mu\). If \(H_0\) is true, then \(\mu=\mu_0\) and the distribution of \(Z\) is known. It is standard normal, exactly for a normal population and approximately for a large sample. If \(H_0\) is false, \(\bar X\) is centred at a value other than \(\mu_0\), and \(Z\) tends to lie far from zero. The value of the test statistic calculated from the data is called the observed value, \(z_{obs}\).

Example 9.4 (Worked example: the hypotheses and the observed value) Shark Tank data A complete test has five steps, which Lecture 10 lists. This example carries out steps 1, 2, and 4. The advisor claims \(\mu_0=15\). The sample of Lecture 7 has \(n=100\) and \(\bar x=12.76\). The population SD, known from the file, is \(\sigma=8.44\).

Step 1. Hypotheses. \(H_0:\mu=15\) versus \(H_1:\mu\ne15\), where \(\mu\) is the mean equity offered in all recorded pitches.
Step 2. Test statistic. \(Z=(\bar X-\mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\). If \(H_0\) is true, it is approximately standard normal, because \(n=100\) is large.
Step 4. Observed value. First the denominator: \(\sigma/\sqrt n=8.44/\sqrt{100}=0.844\). Then
\[
z_{obs}=\frac{12.76-15}{0.844}=\frac{-2.24}{0.844}=-2.65.
\]

The sample mean lies 2.65 standard deviations of the sample mean below the advisor’s figure. Steps 3 and 5, the critical value and the conclusion, follow in Lecture 10.

mu_0    <- 15
sd_xbar <- sigma_equity / sqrt(n)    # standard deviation of the sample mean
z_obs   <- (x_bar - mu_0) / sd_xbar
t_obs   <- (x_bar - mu_0) / se       # the same with s in place of sigma

c(distance = x_bar - mu_0, sd_of_sample_mean = sd_xbar, z_obs = z_obs)

         distance sd_of_sample_mean             z_obs 
       -2.2400000         0.8441425        -2.6535805 

c(standard_error = se, t_obs = t_obs)

standard_error          t_obs 
     0.7707887     -2.9061144 



In a real study \(\sigma\) is unknown. Then \(S\) replaces \(\sigma\), as it did in the interval, and the test statistic is
\[
T=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n},
\]
which has the \(t_{n-1}\) distribution if \(H_0\) is true. Its observed value here is \(t_{obs}=(12.76-15)/0.771=-2.91\). This is the value t = -2.9061 in the R output at the start of this lecture. Lecture 10 first completes the test with \(z_{obs}=-2.65\) and then moves to this version. In practice \(\sigma\) is unknown, so a test for a mean uses \(s\) and \(t\). The figure below shows \(z_{obs}=-2.65\).


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

z_observed <- -2.65
z_ref <- data.frame(z = seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 900))
z_ref$density <- dnorm(z_ref$z)

ggplot(z_ref, aes(z, density)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = z_observed, colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = z_observed - 0.12, y = 0.31,
           label = "observed value", colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.6,
           hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = z_observed - 0.12, y = 0.28,
           label = "z[obs] == -2.65", parse = TRUE, colour = "#D55E00",
           size = 3.8, hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.425,
           label = 'paste("if ", H[0], " is true, Z follows N(0, 1)")',
           parse = TRUE, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.9, y = 0.30,
           label = "how far from zero\nis far enough?",
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.6, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -4:4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.44),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Value of the test statistic Z", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 9.4: The distribution of the test statistic Z if the null hypothesis is true: the standard normal curve. The orange line marks the observed value −2.65, far out in the left tail. The open question is how far from zero the observed value must lie before the null hypothesis is rejected.





Figure 9.4 shows the situation. If the advisor is right, \(Z\) follows the standard normal curve, and \(-2.65\) lies far out in its left tail. But how far is far enough? A value of \(-0.5\) would clearly not be evidence against \(H_0\). A value of \(-10\) clearly would be. Somewhere in between, we must draw a line. We cannot decide where to draw it by looking at the sample. We decide it in advance, based on the probability of a wrong conclusion. That is the subject of Lecture 10.
Here is a first hint of what follows. The 95% interval for \(\mu\) from the Shark Tank case is \((11.23,\ 14.29)\), and it does not contain 15. So, in practice, the interval has already answered the question.






Try it: state the hypotheses





Try this with your neighbour first. For each question, write \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) for a two-sided test, and say which hypothesis is the claim to be established.

Does the proportion of pitches that end in a deal differ from one half?
A commentator claims that sharks close deals in 70% of pitches.
An advisor’s handbook says the typical equity offered is 15%. A founder wants to check the handbook.







Check your answer






\(H_0:p=0.5\) versus \(H_1:p\ne0.5\). The claim to be established is \(H_1\).
\(H_0:p=0.7\) versus \(H_1:p\ne0.7\). The commentator’s figure is the tested value \(p_0=0.7\). The claim to be established is \(H_1\): the deal proportion differs from 0.7.
\(H_0:\mu=15\) versus \(H_1:\mu\ne15\). The claim to be established is \(H_1\). The handbook could be wrong in either direction.








What an interval can and cannot tell you

Precision is not importance. An interval that excludes 15 says that the mean is estimated precisely enough to tell it apart from 15. It does not say that a difference of 2.24 points matters for a decision.
An interval is not a claim about cause. Nothing here says why offers lie below 15%.
A narrow interval does not correct a selection problem. It describes the recorded pitches, not founders in general.

What you can do with it: treat both ends of the interval as possible true values, and ask whether your decision would be the same at each end.




Answering the driving question
For the recorded pitches, the sampling frame, the evidence says yes. The random sample of 100 pitches gives a mean equity offered of 12.76% with a standard error of 0.771 percentage points. The 95% confidence interval is \((11.23,\ 14.29)\)%. It does not contain 15, so at the 5% level we can conclude that the mean differs from 15% and is lower. The test statistic looks at the same distance from the other side. With \(\sigma=8.44\) known, \(z_{obs}=-2.65\): the sample mean lies 2.65 standard deviations of the sample mean below the advisor’s figure. Lecture 10 sets how far from zero is far enough and turns the test statistic into a formal decision. Here the answer can also be checked, because the file is the whole population: \(\mu=13.21\)%, which lies inside the interval and below 15. Whether a difference of about 2 points matters commercially, and what caused it, are separate questions that no interval can answer.

A founder’s decision (invented example)
From 25 orders, the average order value is 9.60 euros with a standard deviation of 2 euros. Order values are roughly normal. You need 9 euros per order to break even on a kitchen lease. The standard error is 2/5 = 0.40 euros. With the supplied value \(t_{0.975,\,24}=2.064\), the 95% confidence interval is 9.60 ± 2.064 × 0.40, from 8.77 to 10.43 euros. The break-even value of 9 euros lies inside the interval, so you cannot conclude that the mean order value differs from 9 euros. The decision: do not sign the lease yet. With 100 orders the standard error falls to 0.20 and the critical value to 1.984. If the mean stays at 9.60 and the standard deviation at 2, the interval then runs from 9.20 to 10.00 and excludes 9. You collect orders for three more weeks and decide then.

Next: We can now report an estimate with a confidence interval, for a mean and for a proportion. We have also stated two hypotheses and measured with a test statistic how far the estimate lies from the tested value. Lecture 10 names the two ways a decision can be wrong and uses them to set the line between “reject” and “do not reject” with a critical value. It writes every test in five steps, reads the same decision from a p-value, and shows what makes wrong decisions rarer. It ends with a first look at a regression table.

title: Lecture 9: The t distribution and confidence intervals
text:
After class
After the lecture, work through all the practice below.

Read the lecture material
Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the main points. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.


Recall questions

Why does replacing \(\sigma\) with the sample SD \(S\) require a t distribution in place of the normal distribution?
Why does the t distribution for one sample mean have \(n-1\) degrees of freedom?
What are the three pieces of a confidence interval?
What is the difference between the interval estimator \((L,U)\) and the confidence interval \((l,u)\)?
Which critical value and which standard error does the interval for a proportion use?
What do \(H_0:\mu=15\) and \(H_1:\mu\ne15\) say? Which of the two conclusions of a test is the strong one?
What is the confidence level a property of: the interval you computed or the procedure?







Check your answers






\(S\) is itself estimated and varies from sample to sample. The heavier tails of the t distribution represent that extra uncertainty.
Before we estimate the spread, we estimate the sample mean. This sets one condition: the deviations must sum to zero. So only \(n-1\) deviations can vary freely.
Estimate, critical value, and standard error.
\((L,U)\) has random bounds. It captures the parameter with probability \(1-\alpha\) before the data are drawn. \((l,u)\) is the pair of numbers calculated from one sample. It either contains the parameter or it does not.
The critical value \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\), for example 1.96 for 95%, and the standard error \(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\).
The null hypothesis states that the population mean equals 15. The alternative states that it differs from 15, in either direction. “Reject \(H_0\)” is the strong conclusion. “Do not reject \(H_0\)” does not show that \(H_0\) is true.
The procedure. With a 95% level, about 95% of intervals built this way from repeated valid samples contain the fixed parameter.






Finish a half-worked example
Re-read the hand-worked interval (Example 9.1). Then complete the same calculation with new invented numbers. A random sample of \(n=25\) customers gives a mean satisfaction of \(\bar x = 42\) points with sample SD \(s = 10\) points. Assume that the scores in the population are roughly normal. The benchmark is 40 points. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean \(\mu\). Supplied value: \(t_{0.975,\,24}=2.064\).
Parts 1 and 2 (given). The formula is \(\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,S/\sqrt n\). It may be used because the population is roughly normal. The given values are \(\bar x=42\), \(s=10\), \(n=25\), \(df=24\), the 95% level, and \(t_{0.975,\,24}=2.064\).
Part 3 (you). Calculate the standard error and the margin of error.
Part 4 (you). Write the interval.
Part 5 (you). Say whether the benchmark of 40 points lies inside the interval, and what you can conclude.






Check your answer





Part 3: the standard error is \(10/\sqrt{25}=2\) points. The margin of error is \(2.064\times 2=4.13\) points. Part 4: the interval is \((42-4.13,\ 42+4.13)=(37.87,\ 46.13)\) points. Part 5: the benchmark of 40 points lies inside the interval. At the 5% level we cannot conclude that the mean satisfaction differs from 40 points. This does not show that the mean equals 40: values up to about 46 points are also compatible with the sample.





Practice
The numbers in tasks 1 to 4 are invented. Write every interval in the five parts.

An app founder measures the length of a session for a random sample of \(n=121\) users. The mean is \(\bar x=18.4\) minutes and the sample SD is \(s=5.5\) minutes. The pitch deck claims a mean of 20 minutes. Construct a 90% confidence interval for the mean session length, and say what it shows about the claim. Supplied value: \(t_{0.95,\,120}=1.658\).
A meal-box start-up asks a random sample of 200 customers whether they would recommend the meal box to a friend. 58 say yes. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all customers who would recommend the meal box. The sector benchmark is 25%. What do you conclude? Use \(z_{0.975}=1.96\).
A bike-repair start-up wants to estimate its mean repair time to within 1.5 minutes, at the 90% confidence level. An earlier study gave an SD of about 8 minutes. How many repairs must be sampled? How many at the 95% level? Use \(z_{0.95}=1.645\) and \(z_{0.975}=1.96\).
A co-working space advertises that members use a desk for 6 hours a day on average. A random sample of \(n=64\) members gives a mean of \(\bar x=5.4\) hours with sample SD \(s=2.0\) hours. Part a: state \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) for a two-sided test of the advertised value. Part b: write the test statistic and calculate its observed value. Say what the value measures. Part c: for task 2, state \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) for a two-sided test of the sector benchmark.
Explain why an interval that excludes a benchmark does not show that the difference is important in practice, or that it has a particular cause.







Check your answers






Part 1: \(\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,S/\sqrt n\), allowed because the sample is random and \(n=121\) is large. Part 2: \(\bar x=18.4\), \(s=5.5\), \(n=121\), \(df=120\), level 90%, so \(\alpha=0.10\) and \(t_{0.95,\,120}=1.658\). Part 3: the standard error is \(5.5/\sqrt{121}=5.5/11=0.5\) minutes, and the margin of error is \(1.658\times0.5=0.83\) minutes. Part 4: \((17.57,\ 19.23)\) minutes. Part 5: the claimed 20 minutes lies outside the interval. At the 10% level we can conclude that the mean session length differs from 20 minutes, and the interval shows that it is shorter.
Part 1: \(\widehat P\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat P(1-\widehat P)/n}\), allowed because \(n\hat p=58\) and \(n(1-\hat p)=142\) are both at least 10. Part 2: 58 customers who say yes, \(n=200\), \(\hat p=58/200=0.29\), level 95%, \(z_{0.975}=1.96\). Part 3: the standard error is \(\sqrt{0.29\times0.71/200}=0.032\), and the margin of error is \(1.96\times0.032=0.063\). Part 4: \((0.227,\ 0.353)\). Part 5: the benchmark 0.25 lies inside the interval. At the 5% level we cannot conclude that the proportion who would recommend the box differs from the sector benchmark.
At the 90% level: \(n\ge(1.645\times8/1.5)^2=8.773^2\approx76.97\), so 77 repairs. At the 95% level: \(n\ge(1.96\times8/1.5)^2=10.453^2\approx109.3\), so 110 repairs. More confidence at the same margin needs more observations. The value 8 is a planning value for \(\sigma\).
Part a. Step 1: \(H_0:\mu=6\) versus \(H_1:\mu\ne6\), where \(\mu\) is the mean daily desk use of all members, in hours. Part b. Step 2: \(T=(\bar X-\mu_0)/(S/\sqrt n)\), which has the \(t_{63}\) distribution if \(H_0\) is true (\(n=64\) is large). Step 4: the standard error is \(2.0/\sqrt{64}=0.25\) hours, so \(t_{obs}=(5.4-6)/0.25=-2.40\). The sample mean lies 2.4 standard errors below the advertised value. Whether that is far enough to reject \(H_0\) is decided in Lecture 10. Part c. \(H_0:p=0.25\) versus \(H_1:p\ne0.25\), where \(p\) is the proportion of all customers who would recommend the box.
An interval that excludes the benchmark says that the estimate is precise enough to tell the parameter apart from the benchmark. Whether the difference is important depends on its size and on the decision. A causal claim needs a suitable study design. A narrow interval gives neither.






Worked exam interpretation: what 95% confidence means
Shark Tank data Exam-style question. Rewrite this claim correctly: “There is a 95% chance that the population mean is in my interval \((11.23, 14.29)\).”






Check a model answer





“The interval \((11.23, 14.29)\) was produced by a procedure that captures the fixed population mean in about 95% of repeated valid samples.” The parameter is fixed. It is the interval endpoints that vary across samples, as in Figure 9.3.





Review: one question each from Lectures 8 and 4

(Lecture 8.) A random sample of \(n=64\) customers has a sample SD of \(s=24\) euros. Calculate the standard error of the sample mean. What happens to it if \(n\) grows to 256 and \(s\) stays the same?
Shark Tank data (Lecture 4.) In the Shark Tank file, \(D\) is the event that a pitch ended with a deal on the show and \(L\) the event that it is from the late seasons. From the 2×2 table of counts, \(P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 0.688\) while \(P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 0.573\). Why are these two numbers different even though both involve the same 505 records?







Check your answers






The standard error is \(24/\sqrt{64}=3\) euros. Four times the sample size halves it to 1.5 euros. This is the square-root rule.
They condition on different events. The first divides the 505 joint records by the 734 late-season records. The second divides the same 505 by the 882 deal records. Changing the event after the bar changes the denominator.






Check the AI
Shark Tank data You asked an AI assistant: “What does the 95% interval from 11.23 to 14.29 for the mean equity offered mean?” It answered:

“It means that 95% of all pitches offer between 11.23% and 14.29% of the company.”

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the Verify step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain.






Check your answer





The interval is about the mean, not about single pitches. In the Shark Tank file, the equity offered (equity_offered_pct) in single pitches ranges from 1% to 100%. The correct reading: the interval was produced by a procedure that captures the mean equity offered in all recorded pitches in about 95% of samples.





Make it yours

Two sentences about your own venture
Think of your EiA venture, or any business you know well. Pick one number of the venture that has an industry benchmark, for example the conversion rate. Decide whether it is a mean \(\mu\) or a proportion \(p\). Sentence 1: which sample could you collect, and what could you claim if the 95% confidence interval does not contain the benchmark? Sentence 2: which decision would change if the interval contains the benchmark?






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus. Churn is the share of subscribers who cancel. “The sector benchmark for churn is 25% per term. From my roughly 120 subscribers I can estimate my churn proportion. A 95% interval that lies entirely below 0.25 would let me claim in my pitch that my customers stay longer than average. If the interval contained 0.25, I would stop presenting customer retention as my advantage and start my pitch with my margin instead.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with Tilly for QM Basic, the course AI assistant: ask it to check whether your parameter is defined on a population you can actually sample.



More practice
For extra exercises on this lecture, with worked solutions, ask Tilly for QM Basic, the course AI assistant. For example: “Give me an extra exercise for Lecture 9. Show the solution only after I send my answer.”
Continue to Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and confidence intervals.
Formula sheet: Lecture 9 formulas.
For a more formal explanation, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 15 and 16.

title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and confidence intervals
text:
Standardising an observation \(x\) from \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) means calculating …
A parameter describes …
An estimator is …
The standard deviation of the sample mean \(\bar X\) is … The standard error of the sample mean is …
The CLT describes …
A written answer for a confidence interval has five parts, in this order: …
The confidence interval for a mean with \(s\) has the formula … It may be used when …
The confidence interval for a proportion has the formula … It may be used when …







Check your preparation






\(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\): the number of population SDs between \(x\) and the mean.
A parameter describes a population.
An estimator is a rule that estimates a parameter from a sample. Its value is random, because the sample is random.
The standard deviation of the sample mean is \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=\sigma/\sqrt n\). The standard error is \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=S/\sqrt n\), with the value \(s/\sqrt n\). It is the estimated standard deviation of \(\bar X\), used when \(\sigma\) is unknown.
The distribution of the sample mean across random samples. It is approximately normal for a large random sample, also when the population is not normal.
Formula, with the reason why it may be used. Given values. Calculations: the standard error, then the margin of error. Interval, with the unit. Conclusion in the words of the question.
\(\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,S/\sqrt n\). The population is normal, or \(n\) is large.
\(\widehat P\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat P(1-\widehat P)/n}\). The condition is \(n\hat p\ge10\) and \(n(1-\hat p)\ge10\).

title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and confidence intervals
text:
In the tutorial
Attempt each task before you open its answer. A complete written answer names the quantity and shows the calculation. It reports the value with its unit and interprets this value in context. It also states one important limit of the model or the data.
Tasks 1 to 9 belong to the tutorial. Tasks 10 to 12 are extra practice for home.
In practice \(\sigma\) is unknown, so an interval for a mean uses \(s\) and a t value. In this book, the values you need are given in the task or on the formula sheet.

Task 1: A normal model in both directions
An invented example. A founder runs an escape room. The time that a team needs to solve the room, \(Y\), is modelled as \(Y\sim N(45,5^2)\), in minutes. The standard deviation is 5 minutes.
Supplied values: \(P(Z\le0.8)=0.7881\), \(P(Z\le1.2)=0.8849\), and the 0.95 quantile \(z_{0.95}=1.645\).

Calculate the probability that a team needs at most 49 minutes.
Calculate the probability that a team needs between 39 and 49 minutes.
The founder wants a time limit that 5% of the teams exceed. Calculate this limit.
Say in one sentence what the supplied quantile 1.645 means for a standard normal variable \(Z\).







Check your answer






Standardise: \(z=(49-45)/5=0.8\). So \(P(Y\le49)=P(Z\le0.8)=0.7881\). About 79% of the teams need at most 49 minutes.
The two z values are \((39-45)/5=-1.2\) and \(0.8\). The supplied values contain only positive z values, so use the symmetry rule and then the complement rule: \(P(Z\le-1.2)=P(Z>1.2)=1-0.8849=0.1151\). Then
\[
P(39\le Y\le49)=P(Z\le0.8)-P(Z\le-1.2)=0.7881-0.1151=0.6730.
\]
About 67% of the teams need between 39 and 49 minutes.
If 5% of the teams exceed the limit, 95% are at or below it. The limit is the 0.95 quantile of \(Y\): \(y=\mu+z\sigma=45+1.645\times5=53.23\) minutes. A limit of about 53 minutes fits.
95% of the values of \(Z\) are at or below 1.645, and 5% are above it.

Parts 1 and 2 go from a value to a probability. Part 3 goes from a probability to a value. One limit: the normal curve is a model. The answers are only as good as the fit of this model to the recorded times.
Verification in R:

c(p_at_most_49 = pnorm(49, mean = 45, sd = 5),
  p_39_to_49 = pnorm(49, mean = 45, sd = 5) - pnorm(39, mean = 45, sd = 5),
  by_hand = 0.7881 - (1 - 0.8849),
  limit = qnorm(0.95, mean = 45, sd = 5),
  limit_by_hand = 45 + 1.645 * 5)

 p_at_most_49    p_39_to_49       by_hand         limit limit_by_hand 
    0.7881446     0.6730749     0.6730000    53.2242681    53.2250000 







Task 2: Population, frame, and claim
A student randomly selects 100 rows from the Shark Tank file and estimates the mean equity offered (equity_offered_pct).

State the population about which this sample allows direct conclusions.
Explain why this sample does not represent all Shark Tank applicants.
Explain why this sample does not represent all US entrepreneurs.
State one change needed to target all US entrepreneurs.







Check your answer





The direct finite population is the 1,441 recorded pitches in completed Seasons 1–16. Applicants who did not appear on television are not in the file, so the frame does not represent all applicants. The show also selects a specialised group of entrepreneurs, not a probability sample of US entrepreneurs. To target all US entrepreneurs, you would need a suitable national sampling frame and a random selection from that frame.





Task 3: Reproduce the realised sample
Shark Tank data The code below draws the sample with seed 123, exactly as in Lecture 7. So you get the same 100 rows when you run it:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

c(
  n = nrow(pitch_sample),
  mean_equity = mean(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  sd_equity = sd(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  q1_equity = unname(quantile(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, 0.25)),
  median_equity = median(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  q3_equity = unname(quantile(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, 0.75)),
  deal_proportion = mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)
)

              n     mean_equity       sd_equity       q1_equity   median_equity 
     100.000000       12.760000        7.707887        8.000000       10.000000 
      q3_equity deal_proportion 
      17.750000        0.640000 


A note on the quartiles in this output. When a quartile falls between two ordered values, R’s quantile() reports a point between them. Here the 75th ordered value is 17 and the 76th is 20, and R reports 17.75. The definition of Lecture 1 holds for every value from 17 to 20. If you take the 75th ordered value, you get 17.

Identify the parameter, estimator, and estimate for the mean equity offered (equity_offered_pct).
Identify the parameter, estimator, and estimate for the deal proportion (deal_on_show).
Calculate the interquartile range (IQR) of the equity offered in the sample from the R output and interpret it. The IQR is defined in Lecture 1.
Explain why a different seed can produce different estimates and a different IQR.







Check your answer





For the equity offered, the parameter is the population mean \(\mu\), the estimator is \(\bar X\), and the estimate is \(\bar x=12.76\)%. For the deal outcome, the parameter is the population proportion \(p\), the estimator is \(\widehat P\), and the estimate is \(\hat p=0.64\). The sample quartiles in the R output are \(Q_1=8\) and \(Q_3=17.75\), so \(\operatorname{IQR}=17.75-8=9.75\) percentage points: the middle half of the initial equity offers in the sample lies between 8% and 17.75%. If you take the 75th ordered value, \(Q_3=17\) and the IQR is \(17-8=9\) percentage points. Both answers are correct when you say how you found \(Q_3\). A different seed selects a different random set of rows. So all sample statistics, including the IQR, can change.
The 25th, 26th, 75th, and 76th ordered values:

sort(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct)[c(25, 26, 75, 76)]

[1]  8  8 17 20







Task 4: Standard errors and a larger sample
Shark Tank data Use the sample output of Task 3.

Calculate the standard error of the sample mean of the equity offered, \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)\).
Calculate the standard error of the sample proportion of deals, \(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)\) (Lecture 8).
Check the success-failure condition for \(\widehat P\).
Predict how each standard error changes if \(n\) increases from 100 to 400 and the spread in the sample stays similar.
In part 1, R calculates the sample SD with sd(). This function divides by \(n-1\). State the value of \(n-1\) here, and explain in one sentence why sd() divides by it.
Explain why the results of parts 1 and 2 are standard errors and not the standard deviations of \(\bar X\) and \(\widehat P\).







Check your answer





\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}=\frac{7.7079}{\sqrt{100}}=0.7708.
\]
\[
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)
=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}
=\sqrt{\frac{0.64(0.36)}{100}}=0.0480.
\]
The standard error of the mean is about 0.77 percentage points of equity. The standard error of the proportion is about 4.8 percentage points of the deal rate. The sample contains 64 successes (deals) and 36 failures (no deal). Both counts are at least 10, so the success-failure condition holds. If \(n\) becomes four times as large, both standard errors are divided by \(\sqrt 4=2\). The divisor is \(n-1=99\). The deviations are measured from the sample mean, so they must sum to zero. As a result, only 99 of them can vary freely. Dividing by 99 removes the downward bias that this causes (Lecture 7).
The standard deviations of the two estimators are \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) and \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). They contain the population values \(\sigma\) and \(p\), which a sample does not give. The standard errors use \(s\) and \(\hat p\) from the sample in their place. A standard error is an estimated standard deviation of an estimator.
Verification in R:

s_equity <- sd(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct)
p_hat <- mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)
c(se_mean = s_equity / sqrt(100),
  se_proportion = sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 100),
  deals = sum(pitch_sample$deal_on_show),
  no_deals = 100 - sum(pitch_sample$deal_on_show),
  se_mean_n400 = s_equity / sqrt(400),
  se_proportion_n400 = sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 400))

           se_mean      se_proportion              deals           no_deals 
         0.7707887          0.0480000         64.0000000         36.0000000 
      se_mean_n400 se_proportion_n400 
         0.3853943          0.0240000 







Task 5: One pitch versus one mean
Shark Tank data Suppose the population mean of the equity offered is \(\mu=13.21\)%, the population SD is \(\sigma=8.44\) percentage points. You draw independent random samples of \(n=100\) pitches. Supplied values: \(P(Z\le 2.12)=0.983\) and \(P(Z\le 0.21)=0.583\).

State the approximate sampling distribution of \(\bar X\), with the standard deviation of the sample mean.
Calculate \(P(\bar X>15)\).
A classmate models a single pitch as \(X\sim N(13.21, 8.44^2)\) and calculates \(P(X>15)\). Compute that value too, and explain why the two answers are so different.
The equity offered is strongly right-skewed (Lecture 1). So which of the two calculations uses a bad model? And why does the CLT still justify the calculation in part 2?







Check your answer





The CLT gives approximately \(\bar X\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(13.21,\,8.44^2/100)\). The standard deviation of the sample mean is \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=8.44/\sqrt{100}=0.844\) percentage points. Therefore
\[
P(\bar X>15)
=1-P\!\left(Z\le\frac{15-13.21}{0.844}\right)
=1-P(Z\le2.12)
\approx0.017.
\]
For a single pitch, \(z=(15-13.21)/8.44\approx0.21\), so \(P(X>15)\approx1-0.583\approx0.42\). The mean of 100 pitches varies ten times less than one pitch (\(\sigma/\sqrt{100}\)), so 15 is an ordinary value for one pitch but an extreme value for a mean of 100. A normal curve is symmetric and the equity offered is strongly right-skewed. So the normal model for a single pitch in part 3 is a bad model. The CLT concerns the sample mean. The mean of 100 independent draws has a nearly normal sampling distribution, even when the population is skewed. This is why the calculation in part 2 is justified.
Verification in R:

sd_mean <- 8.44 / sqrt(100)
c(sd_of_mean = sd_mean,
  z_mean = (15 - 13.21) / sd_mean,
  p_mean_above_15 = 1 - pnorm(15, mean = 13.21, sd = sd_mean),
  z_single = (15 - 13.21) / 8.44,
  p_single_above_15 = 1 - pnorm(15, mean = 13.21, sd = 8.44))

       sd_of_mean            z_mean   p_mean_above_15          z_single 
       0.84400000        2.12085308        0.01696708        0.21208531 
p_single_above_15 
       0.41602024 







Task 6: The exact normal case and the CLT
An invented example. A founder makes scented candles. The burn time of one candle, \(X\), is modelled as \(X\sim N(40,6^2)\), in hours. A tester burns a random sample of \(n=9\) candles and records the sample mean \(\bar X\). Supplied values for the whole task:
P(Z <= 0.6) = 0.7257
P(Z <= 1.8) = 0.9641
P(Z <= 2.5) = 0.9938

State the distribution of \(\bar X\) for \(n=9\), with its mean and its standard deviation. Explain why you may use this distribution although the sample is small.
Calculate the probability that one candle burns less than 36.4 hours.
Calculate the probability that the mean burn time of the 9 candles is below 36.4 hours.
Explain in one sentence why the answers to parts 2 and 3 differ.

The founder also looks at the orders in her web shop. The value of one order is strongly right-skewed: most orders are small and a few are very large. The mean is \(\mu=45\) euros and the standard deviation is \(\sigma=30\) euros.

For a random sample of \(n=100\) orders, calculate the probability that the sample mean is above 52.50 euros. Name the result (the theorem) that allows this calculation.
Explain why you cannot do the same calculation for a random sample of 9 orders.







Check your answer






The population is normal. Then the sample mean is exactly normal for every sample size, also for a small one (Lecture 8): \(\bar X\sim N(40,\,6^2/9)\). Its mean is 40 hours and its standard deviation is \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=6/\sqrt9=2\) hours.
One candle: \(z=(36.4-40)/6=-0.6\). With the symmetry rule and the complement rule, \(P(X<36.4)=P(Z\le-0.6)=1-0.7257=0.2743\).
The mean of 9 candles: \(z=(36.4-40)/2=-1.8\). So \(P(\bar X<36.4)=P(Z\le-1.8)=1-0.9641=0.0359\).
The mean of 9 candles varies three times less than one candle, so 36.4 hours is an ordinary value for one candle (about 27%) and an unusual value for the mean of 9 candles (about 4%).
The population is not normal, but \(n=100\) is large. The CLT gives approximately \(\bar X\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(45,\,30^2/100)\), with \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=30/\sqrt{100}=3\) euros. Then \(z=(52.50-45)/3=2.5\) and \(P(\bar X>52.50)\approx1-0.9938=0.0062\).
The order values are not normal, so the exact normal case does not hold. A sample of 9 is too small for the CLT. No result of Lecture 8 gives the distribution of \(\bar X\) in this case.

Verification in R:

c(sd_mean_9 = 6 / sqrt(9),
  p_one_below_36.4 = pnorm(36.4, mean = 40, sd = 6),
  p_mean_below_36.4 = pnorm(36.4, mean = 40, sd = 6 / sqrt(9)),
  sd_mean_100 = 30 / sqrt(100),
  p_mean_above_52.50 = 1 - pnorm(52.50, mean = 45, sd = 30 / sqrt(100)))

         sd_mean_9   p_one_below_36.4  p_mean_below_36.4        sd_mean_100 
       2.000000000        0.274253118        0.035930319        3.000000000 
p_mean_above_52.50 
       0.006209665 







Task 7: A proportion through the CLT
Shark Tank data The deal proportion (deal_on_show) in the Shark Tank file is \(p=0.612\). A random sample of \(n=100\) pitches is planned, with sample deal proportion \(\widehat P\). Supplied value: \(P(Z\le -2.30)=0.011\).

Calculate the standard deviation of the sample proportion, \(\operatorname{SD}(\widehat P)\), and check the success-failure condition.
State the approximate sampling distribution of \(\widehat P\).
Approximate the probability that the sample shows a deal rate of at most 50%, that is, \(P(\widehat P\le0.50)\).
Interpret the result in one sentence.







Check your answer





Here \(p\) is given, so the result is a standard deviation and not a standard error: \(\operatorname{SD}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{0.612(0.388)/100}\approx0.0487\). The expected counts are \(np=61.2\) and \(n(1-p)=38.8\), both at least 10. So \(\widehat P\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(0.612,\,0.0487^2)\). Standardise:
\[
z=\frac{0.50-0.612}{0.0487}\approx-2.30,
\qquad
P(\widehat P\le0.50)\approx P(Z\le-2.30)\approx0.011.
\]
If the deal proportion in the file is 61.2%, only about 1% of random samples of 100 pitches would show a deal rate at or below 50%. Such a sample would be surprising. Lecture 10 builds the hypothesis test on this idea.
Verification in R:

sd_phat <- sqrt(0.612 * 0.388 / 100)
c(sd_of_phat = sd_phat,
  expected_deals = 100 * 0.612,
  expected_no_deals = 100 * 0.388,
  z = (0.50 - 0.612) / sd_phat,
  p_at_most_050 = pnorm(0.50, mean = 0.612, sd = sd_phat))

       sd_of_phat    expected_deals expected_no_deals                 z 
       0.04872946       61.20000000       38.80000000       -2.29840442 
    p_at_most_050 
       0.01076939 







Task 8: A confidence interval for a mean
An invented example. A founder runs a bouldering gym. Her business plan assumes that a visit lasts 120 minutes on average. She draws a random sample of 16 visits from the 5,000 visits of last year in the check-in system. The sample has a mean of 136 minutes and a standard deviation of \(s=28\) minutes. The visit times are roughly normally distributed. Supplied values: \(t_{0.95,\,15}=1.753\), \(t_{0.975,\,15}=2.131\), and \(t_{0.995,\,15}=2.947\). The formula sheet does not list \(df=15\), so the task gives these values here.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean visit time of last year. Write the five parts of the exam procedure for a mean (Lecture 9). In part 5, say what the interval tells you about the 120 minutes in the business plan.
Construct the 99% confidence interval. Only parts 2 to 5 change.
Construct the 90% confidence interval. Again only parts 2 to 5 change.
Compare the three conclusions about the 120 minutes, and explain how the width of the interval changes with the confidence level.







Check your answer





The 95% interval in five parts:

Formula. \(\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,S/\sqrt n\). It may be used because the visit times are roughly normal. The sample is small, so a large \(n\) is not the reason here.
Given values. \(\bar x=136\) minutes, \(s=28\) minutes, \(n=16\), \(df=15\). The confidence level is 95%, so \(\alpha=0.05\) and the critical value is \(t_{0.975,\,15}=2.131\).
Calculations. The standard error is \(s/\sqrt n=28/\sqrt{16}=7\) minutes. The margin of error is \(2.131\times7=14.92\) minutes.
Interval. \((136-14.92,\ 136+14.92)=(121.08,\ 150.92)\) minutes.
Conclusion. The value 120 minutes lies outside the interval. At the 5% level we can conclude that the mean visit time of last year differs from 120 minutes. The whole interval lies above 120, so visits last longer than the plan assumes. The lower end is 121.08 minutes, only about 1% above 120. So the difference may be small.

The 99% interval, parts 2 to 5:

Given values. As before, but the confidence level is 99%, so \(\alpha=0.01\) and the critical value is \(t_{0.995,\,15}=2.947\).
Calculations. The standard error stays 7 minutes. The margin of error is \(2.947\times7=20.63\) minutes.
Interval. \((136-20.63,\ 136+20.63)=(115.37,\ 156.63)\) minutes.
Conclusion. The value 120 minutes lies inside the interval. At the 1% level we cannot conclude that the mean visit time differs from 120 minutes.

The 90% interval, parts 2 to 5:

Given values. As before, but the confidence level is 90%, so \(\alpha=0.10\) and the critical value is \(t_{0.95,\,15}=1.753\).
Calculations. The standard error stays 7 minutes. The margin of error is \(1.753\times7=12.27\) minutes.
Interval. \((136-12.27,\ 136+12.27)=(123.73,\ 148.27)\) minutes.
Conclusion. The value 120 minutes lies outside the interval. At the 10% level we can conclude that the mean visit time differs from 120 minutes, and the whole interval lies above 120.

A higher confidence level needs a larger critical value, so the margin of error grows from 12.27 minutes at 90% to 14.92 minutes at 95% and 20.63 minutes at 99%. The 99% interval is about 1.7 times as wide as the 90% interval. With the same sample, we can conclude that the mean differs from 120 minutes at the 10% and the 5% level, but not at the stricter 1% level. For this reason every conclusion names its level. One limit: the interval describes the visits of last year, not the visits of next year.
Verification in R, with the supplied t values:

se_visit <- 28 / sqrt(16)
c(se = se_visit,
  margin_95 = 2.131 * se_visit,
  lower_95 = 136 - 2.131 * se_visit, upper_95 = 136 + 2.131 * se_visit,
  margin_99 = 2.947 * se_visit,
  lower_99 = 136 - 2.947 * se_visit, upper_99 = 136 + 2.947 * se_visit,
  margin_90 = 1.753 * se_visit,
  lower_90 = 136 - 1.753 * se_visit, upper_90 = 136 + 1.753 * se_visit,
  width_99_over_90 = 2.947 / 1.753)

              se        margin_95         lower_95         upper_95 
        7.000000        14.917000       121.083000       150.917000 
       margin_99         lower_99         upper_99        margin_90 
       20.629000       115.371000       156.629000        12.271000 
        lower_90         upper_90 width_99_over_90 
      123.729000       148.271000         1.681118 

c(t_95 = qt(0.95, df = 15), t_975 = qt(0.975, df = 15),
  t_995 = qt(0.995, df = 15),
  low_end_above_120_in_percent = 100 * (121.08 - 120) / 120)

                        t_95                        t_975 
                    1.753050                     2.131450 
                       t_995 low_end_above_120_in_percent 
                    2.946713                     0.900000 







Task 9: A confidence interval for a proportion
An invented example. A founder sells sneakers online. Her parcel service reports that customers return 15% of all sneaker orders. Last year her shop had 6,000 orders. She draws a random sample of 400 of these orders. Customers returned 40 of these 400 orders. Let \(p\) be the proportion of returned orders among all 6,000 orders.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(p\). Write the five parts of the exam procedure for a proportion (Lecture 9), with the check of the condition. Check the 10% condition first. In part 5, say what the interval tells you about the 15% reported by the parcel service.
The founder says: “My return rate is 10%, so I am 5 percentage points below the 15%.” Assess this sentence.
State the formula of the standard deviation of \(\widehat P\) and explain why you cannot calculate it here.







Check your answer





The sample contains 400 of the 6,000 orders, that is 6.7%. This is at most 10%, so we may treat the sample as iid.
The interval of part 1 in five parts:

Formula. \(\widehat P\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat P(1-\widehat P)/n}\). The condition holds: \(n\hat p=40\) and \(n(1-\hat p)=360\) are both at least



Given values. 40 returned orders, \(n=400\), \(\hat p=40/400=0.10\). The confidence level is 95%, so \(z_{0.975}=1.960\).
Calculations. The standard error is \(\sqrt{0.10\times0.90/400}=\sqrt{0.000225}=0.015\). The margin of error is \(1.960\times0.015=0.0294\).
Interval. \((0.10-0.0294,\ 0.10+0.0294)=(0.071,\ 0.129)\), that is, from 7.1% to 12.9% of the orders.
Conclusion. The value 0.15 lies outside the interval. At the 5% level we can conclude that her proportion of returned orders differs from 15%. The whole interval lies below 0.15.

Part 2. The sentence treats the estimate as the exact rate. The 10% is the estimate from 400 orders. The plausible values run from 7.1% to 12.9%. So her return rate is between 2.1 and 7.9 percentage points below the 15%.
Part 3. The standard deviation of the sample proportion is \(\operatorname{SD}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). It contains the unknown \(p\), which is the number that the interval tries to estimate. The standard error uses \(\hat p\) in its place.
Verification in R:

p_hat_returns <- 40 / 400
se_returns <- sqrt(p_hat_returns * (1 - p_hat_returns) / 400)
c(p_hat = p_hat_returns,
  successes = 400 * p_hat_returns, failures = 400 * (1 - p_hat_returns),
  se = se_returns, margin = 1.960 * se_returns,
  lower = p_hat_returns - 1.960 * se_returns,
  upper = p_hat_returns + 1.960 * se_returns,
  sample_share_of_orders = 400 / 6000,
  below_15_at_most = 0.15 - (p_hat_returns - 1.960 * se_returns),
  below_15_at_least = 0.15 - (p_hat_returns + 1.960 * se_returns))

                 p_hat              successes               failures 
            0.10000000            40.00000000           360.00000000 
                    se                 margin                  lower 
            0.01500000             0.02940000             0.07060000 
                 upper sample_share_of_orders       below_15_at_most 
            0.12940000             0.06666667             0.07940000 
     below_15_at_least 
            0.02060000 







Task 10: A uniform model (extra practice for home)
An invented example. A founder runs a studio that prints T-shirts for student associations. The time to print one order, \(X\), is equally likely to be anywhere between 20 and 60 minutes: \(X\sim U(20,60)\).

A colleague sketches the density as a flat line at height 0.02 between 20 and 60 minutes, and zero elsewhere. Show that this is not a valid density, and give the correct height.
Calculate \(P(30\le X\le45)\).
Calculate \(P(X>50)\).
Calculate \(P(10\le X\le30)\). Note that a part of this interval lies outside the possible values of \(X\).
State \(P(X=40)\). Then explain why the height of the density is not a probability.







Check your answer






A valid density is never negative and has a total area of 1. The sketch is never negative, but its area is \((60-20)\times0.02=0.8\), not 1. The correct height is \(1/(60-20)=0.025\) per minute. Then the area is \(40\times0.025=1\).
A probability is an area: width times height. So \(P(30\le X\le45)=(45-30)\times0.025=0.375\).
\(P(X>50)=(60-50)\times0.025=0.25\).
The density is zero below 20 minutes, so only the part from 20 to 30 counts: \(P(10\le X\le30)=(30-20)\times0.025=0.25\). A calculation with the full width of 20 minutes gives 0.5, which is wrong.
\(P(X=40)=0\). A single value has width zero, so the area above it is zero. The height 0.025 is a probability per minute. It becomes a probability only when you multiply it by a width in minutes.

Verification in R:

c(area_of_sketch = (60 - 20) * 0.02,
  correct_height = 1 / (60 - 20),
  p_30_to_45 = punif(45, min = 20, max = 60) - punif(30, min = 20, max = 60),
  p_above_50 = 1 - punif(50, min = 20, max = 60),
  p_10_to_30 = punif(30, min = 20, max = 60) - punif(10, min = 20, max = 60))

area_of_sketch correct_height     p_30_to_45     p_above_50     p_10_to_30 
         0.800          0.025          0.375          0.250          0.250 







Task 11: A sample size for a target margin of error (extra practice for home)
The founder of the bouldering gym in Task 8 plans a new and larger sample. She wants to estimate the mean visit time with a margin of error of at most 5 minutes. She uses the sample SD of Task 8 as a planning value: \(\sigma=28\) minutes.

Calculate the sample size that she needs at the 95% level (\(z_{0.975}=1.960\)).
Calculate the sample size for a margin of 2.5 minutes at the 95% level. Compare it with part 1.
Calculate the sample size for a margin of 5 minutes at the 99% level (\(z_{0.995}=2.576\)).







Check your answer





The formula of Lecture 9, with \(m\) the margin of error, is
\[
n\ge\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma}{m}\right)^2 .
\]

\(n\ge(1.960\times28/5)^2=10.976^2\approx120.5\), so she needs 121 visits. Always round up: with 120 visits the margin would be slightly above 5 minutes.
\(n\ge(1.960\times28/2.5)^2=21.952^2\approx481.9\), so 482 visits. Half the margin needs about four times the sample.
\(n\ge(2.576\times28/5)^2=14.4256^2\approx208.1\), so 209 visits. More confidence with the same margin needs more observations: 209 in place of 121.

The planning value is a guess. If the true \(\sigma\) is larger than 28 minutes, the margin of the new sample will be larger than planned.
Verification in R:

n_needed <- c(margin_5_at_95 = (1.960 * 28 / 5)^2,
              margin_2.5_at_95 = (1.960 * 28 / 2.5)^2,
              margin_5_at_99 = (2.576 * 28 / 5)^2)
n_needed

  margin_5_at_95 margin_2.5_at_95   margin_5_at_99 
        120.4726         481.8903         208.0979 

ceiling(n_needed)

  margin_5_at_95 margin_2.5_at_95   margin_5_at_99 
             121              482              209 







Task 12: A value for a sample mean (extra practice for home)
An invented example. A founder sells granola in bags of 250 grams. The filling machine puts \(X\sim N(250,4^2)\) grams into one bag. Every hour she weighs a random sample of \(n=16\) bags and calculates the sample mean \(\bar X\). She wants an alarm value \(a\): she checks the machine when \(\bar X>a\). When the machine works as described, only 5% of the hourly samples may give an alarm. Supplied value: the 0.95 quantile of \(Z\) is \(z_{0.95}=1.645\).

State the distribution of \(\bar X\), with its standard deviation.
Calculate the value \(a\) with \(P(\bar X>a)=0.05\).
Would the same rule make sense with single bags instead of the mean of 16 bags? Calculate the value for a single bag and compare.







Check your answer






The population is normal, so the sample mean is exactly normal: \(\bar X\sim N(250,\,4^2/16)\), with \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=4/\sqrt{16}=1\) gram.
If 5% of the sample means lie above \(a\), then 95% lie at or below it. So \(a\) is the 0.95 quantile of \(\bar X\): \(a=250+1.645\times1=251.65\) grams.
For a single bag the value is \(250+1.645\times4=256.58\) grams. Single bags vary four times more than the mean of 16 bags. So the mean of 16 bags detects a change in the filling of the machine much earlier. Its alarm value is only 1.65 grams above 250, about 0.7% of the bag weight.

Verification in R:

c(sd_mean = 4 / sqrt(16),
  alarm_mean = qnorm(0.95, mean = 250, sd = 4 / sqrt(16)),
  alarm_by_hand = 250 + 1.645 * 1,
  alarm_single = 250 + 1.645 * 4,
  shift_in_percent = 100 * 1.645 / 250)

         sd_mean       alarm_mean    alarm_by_hand     alarm_single 
          1.0000         251.6449         251.6450         256.5800 
shift_in_percent 
          0.6580

title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and confidence intervals
text:
After class

Individual practice
Do this task alone: no notes, no AI, only the formula sheet. An invented example. A random sample of 64 customers has a mean monthly spending of €82 and a sample SD of €24. Of the 64 customers, 40 renewed their subscription.

Calculate the standard error of the mean spending.
Calculate the standard error of the renewal proportion and check its condition.
State what would happen to both standard errors if the sample size were \(n=256\).
Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean monthly spending of all customers, in the five parts of the exam procedure. The degrees of freedom are 63. Use the closest value on the formula sheet: \(t_{0.975,\,60}=2.000\). The business plan of the founder assumes a mean spending of €90. Say in part 5 what the interval tells you about this value.
Write one sentence that explains the difference between sampling uncertainty and selection bias.
Treat \(\mu=82\) and \(\sigma=24\) as the population values. Use the CLT to approximate the probability that a new sample of 64 customers shows a mean above €85. Supplied value: \(P(Z\le 1)=0.841\).
Use \(\sigma=24\) as a planning value. How many customers must a new survey include to estimate the mean spending with a margin of error of at most €3, at the 95% level (\(z_{0.975}=1.96\))?







Check a model answer





The standard error of the mean is \(24/\sqrt{64}=3\) euros. The renewal estimate is \(\hat p=40/64=0.625\), with standard error \(\sqrt{0.625(0.375)/64}\approx0.0605\). The sample has 40 successes and 24 failures, so the success-failure condition holds. Increasing the sample size from 64 to 256 would halve both standard errors if the spread stayed similar.
The interval for the mean spending in five parts:

Formula. \(\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,S/\sqrt n\). It may be used because \(n=64\) is large.
Given values. \(\bar x=82\) euros, \(s=24\) euros, \(n=64\), \(df=63\). The confidence level is 95%, and the closest value on the formula sheet is \(t_{0.975,\,60}=2.000\).
Calculations. The standard error is \(24/\sqrt{64}=3\) euros. The margin of error is \(2.000\times3=6\) euros.
Interval. \((82-6,\ 82+6)=(76,\ 88)\) euros.
Conclusion. The value 90 euros lies outside the interval. At the 5% level we can conclude that the mean monthly spending differs from 90 euros. The whole interval lies below 90, so customers spend less than the plan assumes: at least 2 euros less, about 2% of 90 euros.

The standard errors and the interval describe random variation from sample to sample, not bias created by an unrepresentative sampling frame. For the new sample, the standard deviation of the sample mean is \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=24/\sqrt{64}=3\) euros and \(\bar X\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(82,3^2)\), so \(z=(85-82)/3=1\) and \(P(\bar X>85)\approx1-P(Z\le1)\approx0.16\). For a margin of €3, \(n\ge(1.96\times24/3)^2=15.68^2\approx245.9\), so the survey needs 246 customers (Lecture 9).
Verification in R:

p_hat_renew <- 40 / 64
c(se_mean = 24 / sqrt(64),
  se_proportion = sqrt(p_hat_renew * (1 - p_hat_renew) / 64),
  t_exact_df63 = qt(0.975, df = 63),
  lower = 82 - 2.000 * 3, upper = 82 + 2.000 * 3,
  below_90_in_percent = 100 * (90 - 88) / 90,
  p_mean_above_85 = 1 - pnorm(85, mean = 82, sd = 3),
  n_for_margin_3 = (1.96 * 24 / 3)^2)

            se_mean       se_proportion        t_exact_df63               lower 
         3.00000000          0.06051536          1.99834054         76.00000000 
              upper below_90_in_percent     p_mean_above_85      n_for_margin_3 
        88.00000000          2.22222222          0.15865525        245.86240000 







Check your understanding
Complete from memory:

A sampling distribution describes …
The standard deviation of a sample mean equals … The standard error of a sample mean equals …
The success-failure condition requires …
The CLT says … becomes approximately normal.
A larger sample does not fix …
A claimed value that lies outside a 95% confidence interval means … A claimed value that lies inside means …







Check your answers






How a statistic would vary across repeated random samples.
\(\sigma/\sqrt n\). The standard error is the estimated version, \(s/\sqrt n\).
\(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10\). For a confidence interval the check uses \(\hat p\).
The sample mean. For a large sample its sampling distribution is approximately normal. The single observations do not become normal.
Selection bias, which comes from the way units entered the frame or the sample.
Outside: at the 5% level we can conclude that the parameter differs from the claimed value. Inside: we cannot conclude that it differs, which is not proof that the claimed value is true.






Make it yours

Two sentences about your own venture
Think of your EiA venture, or any business you know well. Pick one rate or average that you could estimate from about 100 observations, for example a conversion rate, the average value of a purchase, or a renewal share. Then write two sentences. First state the standard error that you would roughly expect, and the 95% interval that follows from it. Then name one claimed value that your interval would rule out. Lecture 10 turns this idea into a hypothesis test.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student venture that sells boxes of ready-made meals on campus. “If 60 of 100 customers renew, the standard error of the renewal share is about 5 percentage points, so my 95% interval runs from roughly 50% to 70%. A claim that only 45% renew would lie outside this interval.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with Tilly for QM Basic, the course AI assistant: ask it to check the standard error and the interval for your own numbers.



More practice
For extra exercises on the lectures that this tutorial covers, with worked solutions, ask Tilly for QM Basic, the course AI assistant. For example: “Give me an extra exercise for Tutorial 3. Show the solution only after I send my answer.”
Continue to Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and a first look at regression.

title: Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and a first look at regression
text:
Video preparation Review Introduction to Hypothesis Testing and watch Examples Identifying Type I and Type II Errors. Focus on two-sided tests, decision errors, and why “do not reject” is not “accept.” All links are also listed in the External Video Guide. The videos explain key ideas in another way and can use a different notation. The lecture material and its notation always come first.



Write the two hypotheses of that test.
Say in one sentence what the number \(-2.65\) measures.
Guess: if the advisor’s figure were right, would a value this far from zero be common or rare?







Check your preparation





\(H_0:\mu=15\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne15\), where \(\mu\) is the mean of the equity offered among all 1,441 pitches in the Shark Tank file. The statistic says that the sample mean, 12.76, lies 2.65 standard deviations of the sample mean below 15. Such a value would be rare: the central 95% of the standard normal distribution lies between \(-1.96\) and \(1.96\). The lecture material turns this into a decision rule.
