title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
Before class
Do all the preparation below before class.
Derive the two lines. In the model \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2D+\beta_3XD+\varepsilon\) with a dummy variable \(D\in\{0,1\}\), write the line for \(D=0\) and the line for \(D=1\).
Predict. Answer this question before you come to class: how many separate numbers do you need to fully describe a picture of two straight lines with different slopes? Choose one answer. You will find the answer in the lecture material.
Shark Tank data R warm-up. Build the variables for the analysis. The code uses the same known_gender subset as Lecture 5. It adds a dummy women and a centred season season_c, which is the season minus the mean season. It then fits one line of equity offered on season for each group and draws both lines. Bring the plot:
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)

plot(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = known_gender,
     pch = 16, col = "grey80")
abline(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season,
          data = subset(known_gender, women == 0)),
       col = "#0072B2", lwd = 3)
abline(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season,
          data = subset(known_gender, women == 1)),
       col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3)
Code along (bring your laptop). Bring a charged laptop with RStudio and the course project open. All the code of the lecture is in this chapter, ready to copy. You can run each step yourself during the lecture and get the same numbers and figures.
If you are not sure about products, powers, or centring, review Mathematics Refresher: products, interactions, and combined effects and polynomial terms.

title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
Video preparation Watch Stanford Statistical Learning 3.5 Extensions of the Linear Model and 7.1 Polynomials and Step Functions. Focus on why an interaction changes a slope, and why a model with a quadratic term (a squared predictor) is still a linear regression. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide. The videos explain key ideas in another way and can use a different notation. The lecture material and its notation always come first.








Check your preparation





For \(D=0\): \(E[Y\mid X,D=0]=\beta_0+\beta_1X\). For \(D=1\): \(E[Y\mid X,D=1]=(\beta_0+\beta_2)+(\beta_1+\beta_3)X\). Setting \(D=1\) shifts the intercept by \(\beta_2\) and the slope by \(\beta_3\).

title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
Lecture material
This section adds two terms to the regression model. An interaction term lets a slope differ between two groups, or change with the value of another predictor. A quadratic term lets a slope change along the predictor itself.

Stanford explanations (review): 3.5 Extensions of the Linear Model and 7.1 Polynomials and Step Functions.


Start with a founder’s question
Does advertising work equally well in every week? Does a trend go on in a straight line forever? Often the answer is “it depends”. The two tools of this lecture let you check this in the data. An interaction lets a slope differ between groups. A curve lets a slope change as the predictor grows.


The picture before the formula
In every model so far, all groups had the same slope. Lecture 5 let the height of the line differ between groups. Now the slope may differ as well. Start with the picture in Figure 6.1:


See the R code for this figure
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1), las = 1)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), bty = "n",
     xlab = "Predictor X", ylab = "Outcome Y")
abline(a = 2, b = 0.75, col = "#009E73", lwd = 3)
abline(a = 4.5, b = 0.25, col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
text(8.4, 2 + 0.75 * 8.4 + 0.9, "Group D = 0", col = "#009E73")
text(8.4, 4.5 + 0.25 * 8.4 - 0.8, "Group D = 1", col = "#D55E00")
par(old_par)








Figure 6.1: Two groups, two lines, different slopes (an invented picture). How many numbers do you need to describe this picture completely?





This answers the prediction question from before class: four numbers, an intercept and a slope for each line. The interaction model writes the same four numbers in a different way:
\[
E[Y\mid X,D]
=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2D+\beta_3XD.
\]
Each coefficient is one feature of the picture:

\(\beta_0\): where the \(D=0\) line meets the vertical axis
\(\beta_1\): the slope of the \(D=0\) line
\(\beta_2\): how much higher the \(D=1\) line starts
\(\beta_3\): how much steeper the \(D=1\) line is.

The same in a table with one row per group, as you derived it before class:



Group
Intercept
Slope




\(D=0\)
\(\beta_0\)
\(\beta_1\)


\(D=1\)
\(\beta_0+\beta_2\)
\(\beta_1+\beta_3\)



When \(\beta_3=0\) the two lines are parallel, and the model is the dummy model of Lecture 5 with one common slope.


The interaction coefficient is a difference in slopes

Definition
Interaction term. A term that is the product of two predictors, for example \(X\times D\). It lets the slope of one predictor depend on the value of the other. Its coefficient is a difference in slopes.

In the additive model the slope of \(X\) is the same at every value of the other predictor. With the product \(XD\) in the model, a one-unit increase in \(X\) changes the conditional mean by
\[
\beta_1+\beta_3D.
\]
So \(\beta_3\) is the difference between the slope of the group with \(D=1\) and the slope of the reference category (\(D=0\)). It is not an effect on its own. Its unit combines the two variables. If \(X\) is measured in seasons and \(D\) is a dummy, \(\beta_3\) is in outcome units per season: here, equity percentage points per season, the group with \(D=1\) minus the reference category. The same algebra works when the second variable is a number \(Z\) and not a dummy. The slope of \(X\) is then \(\beta_1+\beta_3Z\), a slope that changes with \(Z\). The section on a continuous moderator below works through this case.
Centring. Centring a predictor means subtracting its mean. With \(XD\) in the model, \(\beta_2\) compares the two groups at \(X=0\). For the Shark Tank data this would be Season 0, which does not exist. Replacing season with
\[
\text{season\_c} = \text{season} - \overline{\text{season}}
\]
moves that comparison to the average season (about 8.8). Centring changes some results and cannot change others:

It changes the meaning and the value of the intercept and of the dummy coefficient. Both now refer to the average season.
It cannot change the fitted values, the residuals, \(R^2\), or the interaction coefficient. The lines are the same lines. Only the place where we compare the two groups has moved.







Check: which printed numbers change when season is centred?





The intercept and the women coefficient change. The interaction coefficient, the ask_1k coefficient, all fitted values, and \(R^2\) do not. You will check this in R in the after-class practice.









Try it: two lines from four coefficients





Try this with your neighbour first. In an invented example, a venture models weekly orders with advertising spend in euros, a dummy for exam weeks, and their interaction: fitted orders = 100 + 0.10 × ads + 15 × exam + 0.12 × ads × exam.
Step 1 (given). In ordinary weeks (exam = 0) the line is 100 + 0.10 × ads.
Step 2 (you). Write the line for exam weeks.
Step 3 (you). Compare the fitted orders at 200 euros of advertising in the two kinds of weeks, and say what the coefficient 0.12 means.






Check your answer





Exam weeks: (100 + 15) + (0.10 + 0.12) × ads = 115 + 0.22 × ads. At 200 euros: 120 orders in an ordinary week and 159 in an exam week. The coefficient 0.12 is the difference between the two slopes: each euro of advertising goes with 0.12 more orders in an exam week than in an ordinary week.








The Shark Tank interaction model
Shark Tank data Now answer the first part of the driving question. In this lecture, women = 1 means that the presenting team is classified as all-women or mixed, and women = 0 means all-men. This split is broader than the three categories of Lecture 5. It does not measure the share of women or the full team behind the venture. As before, we leave out the seven unknown records. The code first builds the variables, as in the R warm-up:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)

interaction_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(interaction_model)


Call:
lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, 
    data = known_gender)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-15.871  -4.742  -1.290   3.412  82.689 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    13.6247907  0.3354522  40.616  < 2e-16 ***
season_c       -0.7993817  0.0663226 -12.053  < 2e-16 ***
women           0.8069665  0.4117061   1.960   0.0502 .  
ask_1k         -0.0026776  0.0005834  -4.590 4.83e-06 ***

Step 1: the two lines. Fill in the table with one row per group. At the average requested amount, with \(\text{season\_c}\) as the predictor:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{all-men teams: } & \widehat{\text{equity}} = 12.866 - 0.799\times\text{season\_c},\\
\text{teams with women: } & \widehat{\text{equity}} = (12.866+0.807) + (-0.7994-0.0615)\times\text{season\_c}\\
& \phantom{\widehat{\text{equity}}} = 13.673 - 0.861\times\text{season\_c}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 2: one sentence per coefficient.

season_c (\(-0.799\)). Among all-men teams, one season later is associated with an equity offered that is on average 0.80 percentage points lower, at the same requested amount. This is the slope of the reference category only.
season_c:women (\(-0.061\)). Per one season more, the equity offered by teams with women falls 0.061 percentage points more than that of all-men teams. This is the difference between the two slopes. It is about 8% of the all-men slope.
women (\(0.807\)). In the average season (about 8.8), teams with women are fitted to offer about 0.81 percentage points more equity than all-men teams, at the same requested amount. With the interaction in the model, this difference holds only where \(\text{season\_c}=0\). In other seasons the gap is \(0.807-0.061\times\text{season\_c}\).
ask_1k (\(-0.0027\)). A request that is $1,000 higher is associated with an equity offered that is on average 0.0027 percentage points lower, in both groups. Per $100,000 more, this is about 0.27 percentage points.
The intercept (\(13.62\)) is the fitted equity offered for all-men teams in the average season with a requested amount of $0. The smallest request in the data is $10,000, so the intercept has no useful meaning of its own.

Step 3: how large is it? In the average season, all-men teams are fitted to offer 12.87% and teams with women 13.67%. The gap is 0.81 percentage points. Measured as a percent of the all-men level, the same gap is about 6%. So “0.81 percent more” would be wrong. The coefficient is a difference in percentage points.
Why does the model use season_c and not season? The dummy coefficient always compares the groups at \(X=0\). Without centring, \(X=0\) would be Season 0, a season outside the data. Centring moves the comparison to the average season, where there are many pitches.

The interaction estimate is \(-0.061\) equity percentage points per season, with a p-value of about 0.520. The difference is small, about 8% of the all-men slope (Example 6.1). Draw two conclusions from this result. First, the model gives no evidence that the season trend differs between the two groups. Second, the model does not prove that the two slopes are equal. The estimate is imprecise (standard error about 0.096), so the data are consistent with a somewhat steeper trend and also with a somewhat flatter trend for teams with women. No evidence of a difference is not proof of no difference.

A continuous moderator
The second variable of an interaction need not be a dummy. It can be any number \(Z\), such as a price, a firm size, or a number of stores. The model is
\[
E[Y\mid X,Z]=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2Z+\beta_3XZ,
\]
and a one-unit increase in \(X\) changes the conditional mean by \(\beta_1+\beta_3Z\). There are now not two lines but one line for every value of \(Z\).

Definition
Moderator. A variable \(Z\) that changes the slope of another predictor \(X\) through the interaction term \(XZ\). The slope of \(X\) at one value of \(Z\), \(\beta_1+\beta_3Z\), is called the conditional effect of \(X\) at that value.

The name “conditional effect” is standard, but it is still a fitted slope. It is a causal effect only when the design of the study allows a causal reading. Two coefficients now need care. \(\beta_1\) is the slope of \(X\) only where \(Z=0\), and \(\beta_2\) is the slope of \(Z\) only where \(X=0\). If zero lies outside the data, neither number describes any real case. The coefficients \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) are often called the main effects. With \(XZ\) in the model they are conditional too. Centring \(Z\) makes \(\beta_1\) the slope of \(X\) at the mean of \(Z\).

The hierarchy principle and the * shorthand
The hierarchy principle says: if a model contains \(XD\), keep both \(X\) and \(D\) in the model, even when one of them is not significant on its own. The same holds for \(XZ\) with a continuous moderator \(Z\). The terms \(X\) and \(D\) define the two lines, and the interaction describes the difference between these lines. If you leave out \(D\), the model forces both lines to start at the same height. This distorts the interaction coefficient. The * shorthand in an R formula follows the principle for you:

lm(y ~ x * z, data = df)  # x * z expands to x + z + x:z



Moderation and mediation
Two words often appear in business research about a third variable: a moderator and a mediator. They describe different roles, and a regression handles them in different ways.
Moderation first. A moderator changes the strength or the direction of the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\). With a moderator, the answer to “how is \(X\) related to \(Y\)?” is “it depends on \(Z\)”. In a regression, moderation shows up as an interaction term. You have seen two cases. In Example 6.1 the moderator is a dummy, the women group, and the season slope differs between two groups. In Example 6.2 the moderator is a number, the number of stores, and the marketing slope grows with every extra store. A moderator can also reverse a relationship, for example a price cut that raises orders for students and lowers them for a luxury segment.

Definition
Mediator. A variable \(M\) that lies on the path from \(X\) to \(Y\): \(X\) affects \(M\), and \(M\) affects \(Y\). The part of the effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) that runs through \(M\) is called the indirect effect.

Take marketing spending (\(X\)), website visits (\(M\)), and sales (\(Y\)). Marketing brings visitors to the website, and visitors buy. Marketing can also raise sales in other ways, for example through people who see an advert and buy in a shop. Figure 6.4 shows the two paths. Three effects describe them:

the total effect: how much \(Y\) changes when \(X\) changes, by all paths together
the direct effect: the part that does not run through \(M\)
the indirect effect: the part that runs through \(M\).

The total effect is the direct effect plus the indirect effect.

Curvature: polynomials are still linear regression
An interaction term lets the slope of \(x\) differ by group or change with a moderator. A quadratic term, defined below, lets the slope change as \(x\) itself changes. Both add one new column to the data, a product or a square. In both, you read two coefficients together.
Shark Tank data Is the season trend a straight line at all? To let it bend, add the square of the predictor.

Definition
Quadratic term. The square of a predictor, \(x^2\), added to a model that also contains \(x\). It lets the fitted line bend, so the slope changes with \(x\). A model with powers of a predictor is called a polynomial.

The quadratic conditional mean
\[
E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2
\]
is curved in \(x\), but it is linear in the unknown coefficients \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\). Linearity in the coefficients is all that lm() requires. The square is one more column of data.
What changes is how you read the output. The slope is no longer one number. Moving from \(x\) to \(x+1\) changes the conditional mean by
\[
(\beta_1(x+1)+\beta_2(x+1)^2) - (\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2)
=\beta_1+\beta_2(2x+1).
\]
This change depends on the starting value \(x\). The rule is: never read \(\beta_1\) alone while \(x^2\) is in the model. Calculate fitted changes or graph the curve.

linear_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks)
poly_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k,
                  data = sharks)
summary(poly_season)$coefficients

I() tells R to calculate the square. Without I(), R would read ^ as part of the formula syntax and not as a square. The fitted coefficients are \(\hat\beta_1 \approx -1.713\) for season and \(\hat\beta_2 \approx 0.051\) for I(season^2). Together they describe a steep decline in the early seasons that becomes flatter season by season.

Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The partial F-test for adding I(season^2) gives \(F \approx 20.1\) with a p-value below 0.001. The data show a curve. But the gain in fit is small: adjusted \(R^2\) rises from about 0.186 to about 0.196, one percentage point more of the variation in the equity offered. So also look at the shape of the curve in Figure 6.5:


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
poly_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k,
                  data = sharks)
season_means <- aggregate(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks, mean)
curve_data <- data.frame(season = seq(1, 16, length.out = 200),
                         ask_1k = mean(sharks$ask_1k))
curve_data$fit <- predict(poly_season, newdata = curve_data)

ggplot(season_means, aes(x = season, y = equity_offered_pct)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 16, xmax = 17.6, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey75", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 16, colour = "grey60",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x = season, y = fit),
            colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  annotate("text", x = 16.8, y = max(season_means$equity_offered_pct),
           label = "no data beyond\nseason 16", colour = "#5B6976",
           size = 3, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 16, by = 3)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1, 17.6)) +
  labs(x = "Season", y = "Initial equity offered (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 6.5: Season means of the equity offered (points) and the fitted quadratic curve at the average requested amount. The curve becomes flatter towards the last observed seasons. Beyond Season 16 (shaded) it would turn upward, but there are no data in that region.





The points in Figure 6.5 are the plain means of each season. The curve keeps the requested amount fixed at its sample mean. To extrapolate means to use a fitted model outside the range of the data. Do not extrapolate the quadratic beyond Seasons 1–16. The fitted curve reaches its lowest point just after Season 16 and would rise steeply afterwards. This rise comes from the shape of a quadratic, not from any data, so it is not a forecast.

What flexible terms can and cannot repair

Interactions and curves make the model more flexible. They cannot fix problems in how the data were produced.
Every added term costs precision. Add a term because your question needs it, not because it turns out to be significant.
You can trust a curve only inside the range of the data.

What you can do with it: ask whether a relationship could differ between groups or follow a curve, add that one term, graph the fitted lines, and report combined results.



Answering the driving question
The same trend for every kind of team? The estimated difference in slopes is \(-0.061\) percentage points per season (p \(\approx\) 0.52). The data show no difference between all-men teams and teams with women. They also do not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise.
A straight line? Not quite. The quadratic term is significant (partial \(F \approx 20.1\), p \(<\) 0.001). The fitted decline becomes flatter: from about \(-1.56\) points per season between Seasons 1 and 2 to about \(-0.64\) between Seasons 10 and 11. Use the curve only inside Seasons 1–16.
The founder’s questions at the start of the lecture get the same two kinds of answer. Whether advertising works equally well in every week is a question about an interaction. In the invented example of the Try it task, advertising does not work equally well: the slope is 0.10 orders per euro in ordinary weeks and 0.22 in exam weeks. Whether a trend goes on in a straight line is a question about a curve. The season trend of the equity offered does not go on in a straight line: the fitted drop per season shrinks from about 1.56 to about 0.64 points, and beyond Season 16 the data say nothing.

A founder’s decision (invented example)
You suspect that advertising works better in exam weeks. The model with an interaction gives an advertising slope of 0.10 orders per euro in ordinary weeks and 0.10 + 0.12 = 0.22 in exam weeks. After a price increase, each order now brings 6 euros of margin. So 100 euros of advertising goes with 10 more orders and 60 euros of margin in an ordinary week, which is less than the advertising costs. In an exam week it goes with 22 more orders and 132 euros of margin. The decision: advertise in the exam weeks only. One check first: the interaction of 0.12 has its own interval. If that interval includes zero, the data do not yet show that the two kinds of weeks differ. Then keep spreading the advertising budget over both kinds of weeks for one more study period before you decide.

Next: Tutorial 2 practises Lectures 4–6 with exam-style questions. It ends with one full analysis, from a research question to a conclusion of 150 words. Your thesis asks for this kind of analysis too.

title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
After class
After the lecture, work through all the practice below.

Read the lecture material
Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the main ideas. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly, the course AI assistant.


Recall questions

What does an interaction coefficient measure, and what is its unit in the model with season and the women dummy?
Why centre a predictor before you use it in an interaction, and what can centring never change?
State the hierarchy principle.
Why is a quadratic model still a linear regression model?
Why should you graph a quadratic curve, and why should you not extrapolate it?
In the invented franchise model, marketing is 1.745 and marketing:stores is 0.147, with sales and marketing in €1,000s. What is the slope of marketing in a region with 6 stores, and why does 1.745 alone not describe any region?
A researcher finds that training is related to productivity, and that the relationship is stronger in large firms. A second researcher finds that training raises skills and that skills raise productivity. Which finding is about a moderator and which about a mediator, and how does each appear in a regression?







Check your answers






How the slope of one predictor changes with the value of the other predictor. Here its unit is equity percentage points per season, as a difference between the two groups.
So that the intercept and the dummy coefficient refer to a useful value, such as the sample mean, and not to zero. Centring never changes the fitted values, the residuals, \(R^2\), or the interaction coefficient.
Keep \(X\) and \(D\) in the model whenever their interaction \(XD\) is in it, and keep \(x\) whenever \(x^2\) is in it.
It is linear in the unknown coefficients. The squared column is one more predictor built from the data.
No single coefficient is the slope, so only fitted values or the curve show what the model says. Outside the observed range the curve can turn sharply, and no data support that turn.
\(1.745+0.147\times6\approx2.63\): in a region with 6 stores, €1,000 more marketing is associated with about €2,630 more monthly sales on average. The number 1.745 is the slope at 0 stores. No region has 0 stores, so it is a conditional effect at a value outside the data.
Firm size is a moderator: it changes the slope of training. It appears as an interaction term of training and firm size. Skills are a mediator: they lie on the path from training to productivity. Adding skills to the model shrinks the training coefficient to the direct part, so leave skills out if you want the total effect.






Centring verification
Shark Tank data Fit the interaction model with and without centring season. Check that the fitted values and the interaction coefficient are unchanged, and report which coefficients do change.






Check your answer






sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)

uncentred <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season * women + ask_1k,
                 data = known_gender)
centred <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
               data = known_gender)
all.equal(fitted(uncentred), fitted(centred))

[1] TRUE

c(uncentred = unname(coef(uncentred)["season:women"]),
  centred = unname(coef(centred)["season_c:women"]))

  uncentred     centred 
-0.06145941 -0.06145941 

c(women_uncentred = unname(coef(uncentred)["women"]),
  women_centred = unname(coef(centred)["women"]))

women_uncentred   women_centred 
      1.3465150       0.8069665 


The fitted values agree, and both interaction estimates are about \(-0.061\). The women coefficient changes from about \(1.35\) (a comparison at Season 0, which does not exist) to about \(0.81\) (a comparison at the average season, about 8.8). The intercept changes as well. Centring moved the place where we compare the two groups. It did not move the lines.





Finish a half-worked example: a quadratic change
Shark Tank data Read the worked calculation for Season 5 to Season 6 again (Example 6.4). Then calculate the fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11 in the same model.
Step 1 (given). The formula is \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)\) with \(x=10\), so you multiply \(\hat\beta_2\) by \(21\).
Step 2 (you). Insert \(\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713\) and \(\hat\beta_2\approx0.051\).
Step 3 (you). Compare the result with the Season 5 to 6 change and state in one sentence what the comparison shows about the trend.






Check your answer





\(-1.713+0.051\times21\approx-1.713+1.071\approx-0.64\) percentage points (with the unrounded coefficients: \(\hat\beta_1+21\hat\beta_2=-0.642\)). The drop per season has become smaller, from about \(-1.15\) (Seasons 5–6) to about \(-0.64\) (Seasons 10–11). The decline becomes flatter in later seasons. This is what a positive \(\hat\beta_2\) means.



Now do the next tasks on your own, with new coefficients from an invented example. A model of monthly revenue (€1,000s) on the age of a shop \(x\) (years) reports \(\widehat Y = 40 - 2.00x + 0.060x^2\).

Calculate the fitted change from age 3 to age 4 and from age 8 to age 9.
A colleague reports “revenue falls €2,000 per year of age.” Correct the sentence.
In \(\widehat Y=10+2X+3D-0.5XD\), write the lines of both groups and interpret the interaction coefficient.







Check your answers






Age 3 to 4: \(-2.00+0.060(2\times3+1)=-2.00+0.42=-1.58\), about \(-\text{€}1{,}580\). Age 8 to 9: \(-2.00+0.060\times17=-0.98\), about \(-\text{€}980\).
\(-2.00\) is not the fitted change per year. With \(x^2\) in the model the change depends on age: about \(-1.58\) from age 3 to 4 and about \(-0.98\) from age 8 to 9. The decline becomes weaker as shops get older.
For \(D=0\): \(\widehat Y=10+2X\). For \(D=1\): \(\widehat Y=13+1.5X\). The interaction coefficient \(-0.5\) says that the slope of the \(D=1\) group is 0.5 outcome units per unit of \(X\) smaller than the slope of the \(D=0\) group.






Practice: all steps together
Shark Tank data In Lecture 4 you wrote a paragraph that connects the diagnostics of Lecture 2 to the three-predictor model of the equity offered. Add one argument to that paragraph. Propose either an interaction or a quadratic term for that model. State the question about the business or the data that motivates the term, and say how you would test whether the term belongs in the model.






Check a model answer





A good answer: “The decline over the seasons need not be a straight line. The show was new in the early seasons and pitches became more professional later, so the trend may become flatter. I would add I(season^2). I add the term because of this question about the shape, not because I am searching for a significant result. I would test it with a partial F-test against the nested linear model on the same observations (here \(F\approx20.1\), p \(<\) 0.001). I would also check that adjusted \(R^2\) rises and graph the fitted curve inside Seasons 1–16. Finally, I would report fitted changes from season to season, not the season coefficient alone.” An answer with an interaction is equally good if it names the question and the nested test. An example is the interaction of season with the women dummy, which asks whether the trend differs between the groups. Its test gives \(F\approx0.41\) and p \(\approx\) 0.52, so the term is not kept.





Review: one partial-F question from Lecture 5
Shark Tank data Adding the two gender dummies to the model of equity on season and requested amount reduced the residual sum of squares by 436.25 using 2 degrees of freedom, and the complete model left 82,792 on 1,429 degrees of freedom. Compute the partial F statistic and state the 5% conclusion.






Check your answer





\(F=(436.25/2)/(82{,}792/1{,}429)=218.1/57.9\approx3.76\), with p \(\approx\) 0.023. At 5%, the two category terms are jointly significant in that model, even though the t-test of the mixed dummy alone is far from significant. Joint tests and individual tests answer different questions.





Worked exam interpretation
Exam-style question. An invented example. A model of the weekly revenue of market stalls (in €100s) on opening hours per week, a dummy for indoor stalls, and their interaction reports hours 1.20, indoor 2.00, hours:indoor -0.50. A student writes: “One more opening hour raises weekly revenue by €120 for all stalls.” Correct the sentence.






Check a model answer





Two corrections. First, with the interaction in the model, 1.20 is the fitted slope of opening hours only for stalls that are not indoor (indoor = 0). For indoor stalls the slope is \(1.20-0.50=0.70\), that is, €70 of weekly revenue per opening hour. There is no single slope for all stalls. Second, “raises” claims causation. These are fitted associations among the sampled stalls, holding the other included terms fixed. The data do not come from an experiment, so they do not show an effect of opening hours.





Check the AI
Shark Tank data You asked an AI assistant: “The interaction has a coefficient of -0.061 and a p-value of 0.52. What do I conclude?” It answered:

“The p-value proves that the season trend is identical for both groups. And the season coefficient of -0.80 is the season trend for all teams.”

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the Verify step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain.






Check your answer





Two errors. A large p-value means the data do not show a difference. It does not prove that the trends are the same, because the estimate is imprecise. And with an interaction in the model, -0.80 is the trend for the group coded 0, the all-men teams. For teams with women it is -0.80 - 0.06 = -0.86.





Make it yours

Two sentences about your own venture
Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Name one relationship in its data whose slope could depend on something else. For example, the response to price may differ by customer segment, the result of a campaign may differ by channel, or growth may become flatter as the business gets larger. Then write two sentences. First, state the interaction or quadratic term you would add and the question behind it. Second, say what a result that is not significant would tell you, and what it would not tell you. There is no wrong answer.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus. “I would add an interaction of advertising spend with exam week, because my question is whether advertising works only when students are on campus. An interaction that is not significant would mean no evidence that the slopes differ. It would not prove that exam weeks make no difference.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant. Ask it to read your two sentences and to check whether you treated “no evidence of a difference” as “proof of no difference”.



More practice
For extra exercises on this lecture, with worked solutions, ask Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant. For example: “Give me an extra exercise for Intermediate Lecture 6. Show the solution only after I send my answer.”
Continue to Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions.
Code sheet: Lecture 6 commands and formulas.
For a more formal treatment, see James et al., An Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Section 3.3.2 and Sections 3.6.4–3.6.6, and Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapter 21.

title: Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions
text:
In the tutorial
Try each task in R before you open the answer. Tasks 1 to 4 use the Shark Tank file, and money is measured in thousands of dollars (ask_1k). First build the data for the analysis. The code is the same as in Lectures 4–6. Tasks 1 to 6 and the regression table belong to the tutorial.

  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")

known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)


Task 1: Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4)
Shark Tank data Fit:

  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words,
  data = sharks
)

Interpret all three slopes with units and with the predictors that are held fixed.
Find out which 95% confidence interval of a coefficient includes zero.
Interpret adjusted \(R^2\) and the overall F-test.
Give two reasons why the coefficients cannot be read as causal effects.







Check your answer





At fixed values of the other included predictors, among the 1,441 recorded pitches: one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less equity offered, an extra $1,000 requested with about 0.0029 percentage points less (about 0.29 points per $100,000), and one additional description word with about 0.128 percentage points less. confint(m1) shows that the interval for the description words, about \((-0.351, 0.095)\), includes zero. \(R^2\approx0.188\): the model explains about 19% of the variation in the equity offered. Adjusted \(R^2\approx0.186\) is almost the same, so the fit does not come from extra predictors that only fit chance variation. The overall F-test (\(F\approx110.6\) on 3 and 1437 df) rejects the null hypothesis that all three slopes are zero. Possible reasons against a causal reading: only selected pitches reach the show, the quality of the venture is not measured, the equity offered may influence the amount requested, and the variables may be measured with error.





Task 2: Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5)

Shark Tank data Name the reference category.
Interpret both dummy coefficients.
State the hypotheses of the partial F-test and decide.
Explain why the partial F-test and the individual t-tests answer different questions.







Check your answer





The reference category is all-men. At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men teams, and mixed teams about 0.12 points more. The unit is percentage points, not percent. The null hypothesis of the partial F-test is that both dummy coefficients are zero. \(F\approx3.76\) and p \(\approx\) 0.023, so we reject the null hypothesis at 5%. The two terms are jointly significant, even though the t-test of the mixed dummy alone (p \(\approx\) 0.82) is far from significant. The F-test asks whether the two terms together improve the model. Each t-test asks about one comparison with the reference category. The categories are broad and the data do not come from an experiment, so the result does not show a causal effect of gender.





Task 3: Interaction (Lecture 6)

m_interaction <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(m_interaction)

Shark Tank data Write the fitted line for women = 0 and for women = 1 at the average requested amount.
Calculate both season slopes.
Interpret the interaction estimate and its p-value without claiming too much in either direction.
Explain what centring does.







Check your answer





At the average requested amount, the fitted line for all-men teams is \(12.866-0.799\,\text{season\_c}\), and for teams with women it is \(13.673-0.861\,\text{season\_c}\), as in Lecture 6. The intercept 12.866 is the intercept 13.625 plus the ask_1k coefficient times the average requested amount, mean(known_gender$ask_1k). For teams with women the intercept is \(12.866+0.807=13.673\) and the slope is \(-0.7994-0.0615=-0.861\). So the season slope is about \(-0.799\) percentage points per season for all-men teams and about \(-0.861\) for teams with women. The estimated difference in slopes is \(-0.061\) percentage points per season with p \(\approx\) 0.520. The model gives no evidence that the season trends differ between the two groups. It also does not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise. Centring makes the women coefficient compare the groups at the average season (about 8.8) and not at Season 0, which does not exist. It changes neither the fitted values nor the interaction estimate.

Check your answer





I() tells R to calculate the square. Without I(), R would read ^ as part of the formula syntax and not as a square. The partial F-test gives \(F\approx20.1\) with p \(<\) 0.001, so the quadratic term improves the model. With \(\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713\) and \(\hat\beta_2\approx0.051\), the change from Season 10 to 11 is \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times10+1)=\hat\beta_1+21\hat\beta_2\approx-0.64\) percentage points. Never read \(\hat\beta_1\) alone while the quadratic term is in the model. Beyond Season 16 the fitted curve turns upward, and no data support that turn. A quadratic curve can change direction sharply outside the observed range.

The numbers in parentheses are standard errors. The stars show the p-value of the two-sided t-test of each coefficient against zero. For self-efficacy, \(t_{obs}=0.38/0.07\approx5.4\). This is far beyond the critical value \(t_{0.975,\,260}\) = qt(0.975, 260) = 1.969, and p is below 0.001, so three stars are correct.

The two added predictors explain a further 16 percentage points of the variation in intentions in this sample. A partial F-test of the two nested models would show whether the two added predictors are jointly significant. It compares model (1) with model (2) on the same 265 students. If you have the data, anova() of the two fitted models gives this test.






Task 6: A/B test, one-way ANOVA, moderator and mediator (Lectures 5 and 6)
(a) An invented A/B test. An online shop for refurbished phones shows 120 new visitors either its current product page (new_page = 0) or a new page with customer videos (new_page = 1). Chance decides which page each visitor sees, 60 visitors per page. The outcome is the value of the first order in euros.

set.seed(21)
# random assignment: 60 zeros (old page) and 60 ones (new page)
new_page <- sample(rep(c(0, 1), each = 60))
# invented order values in euros, with a true effect of 3 euros
order_value <- round(40 + 3 * new_page + rnorm(120, mean = 0, sd = 8), 2)
ab_shop <- data.frame(new_page, order_value)
ab_fit <- lm(order_value ~ new_page, data = ab_shop)
summary(ab_fit)$coefficients

Test in five steps whether the new page changes the mean order value. Explain why \(\hat\beta_1\) estimates the average treatment effect of the new page, and judge its size.
(b) An invented one-way ANOVA. The same shop records the delivery time in hours of 20 orders for each of three couriers.

courier <- factor(rep(c("cycle", "post", "van"), each = 20))
delivery_hours <- round(c(rnorm(20, 20, 6), rnorm(20, 26, 6),
                          rnorm(20, 22, 6)), 1)

courier_fit <- lm(delivery_hours ~ courier, data = deliveries)
coef(courier_fit)

[1] 23.95667

Which regression lies behind this ANOVA table, and what do its two dummy coefficients say? Test at 5% whether the mean delivery time is the same for the three couriers: give \(H_0\), \(F\), both degrees of freedom, and the conclusion.
(c) A meal-kit start-up gives a discount coupon at random to half of its customers. Customers with the coupon order more meal kits. The coupon raises orders more for students than for other customers. The coupon also brings customers to the website more often, and more visits go with more orders. Which variable is a moderator, and which is a mediator? How does each one appear in a regression of orders on the coupon dummy?






Check your answer





(a) The mean order value is 39.09 euros with the old page (the intercept) and \(39.09+3.41=42.50\) euros with the new page.

Hypotheses. \(H_0:\beta_1=0\), the new page has no effect on the mean order value. \(H_1:\beta_1\ne0\). The significance level is 5%.
Test statistic. \(T=\hat\beta_1/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\), with \(df=n-k-1=118\).
Critical value and rejection region. \(t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980\), from qt(0.975, df = 118). Reject \(H_0\) if \(|t_{obs}|\ge1.980\).
Observed value. \(t_{obs}=3.409/1.341\approx2.54\).
Conclusion. \(2.54\ge1.980\), so reject \(H_0\) (p \(\approx\) 0.012). At the 5% level, the new page raises the mean order value.

Chance decided who saw the new page. So the two groups are alike on average in everything else, measured or not, and the only systematic difference is the page. That is why \(\hat\beta_1\approx3.41\) euros estimates the average treatment effect of the new page. It is about 8.7% of the mean order value with the old page.
(b) The ANOVA table comes from the regression of delivery_hours on two dummies, post and van, with cycle as the reference category. The intercept 22.65 hours is the mean of the cycle courier. The post courier takes on average 3.94 hours longer, and the van courier 0.02 hours less. \(H_0:\mu_{\text{cycle}}=\mu_{\text{post}}=\mu_{\text{van}}\) against \(H_1\): at least one mean differs. \(F_{obs}=103.62/35.11\approx2.95\) with \(G-1=2\) and \(n-G=57\) degrees of freedom. The critical value is 3.16, from qf(0.95, 2, 57). Because \(2.95<3.16\) (p \(\approx\) 0.060), do not reject \(H_0\). At the 5% level, the data do not show that the mean delivery time differs between the couriers. This does not prove that the means are equal. The largest difference, 3.95 hours between the post and the van courier, is about 16% of the overall mean of 23.96 hours.
(c) Student status is the moderator: it changes the slope of the coupon. It enters as an interaction, lm(orders ~ coupon * student), and the coefficient of coupon:student is the difference in the coupon effect between students and other customers. Website visits are the mediator: they lie on the path from the coupon to orders. Adding visits, lm(orders ~ coupon + visits), shrinks the coupon coefficient to the direct part. For the total effect of the coupon, leave visits out of the model.

title: Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions
text:
After class

Individual practice
Shark Tank data Build one model of the equity offered (equity_offered_pct) in the Shark Tank file. Use season, the requested amount in $1,000s, the presenting team, and one extension that you can justify: an interaction of season with the dummy women, or a quadratic term in season next to the three known team categories (gender).
Your answer must include:

a precise research question
the code that prepares the data, so that someone else can repeat it
one graph of the data before you fit the model
the R formula and the model summary. If you compare several models, show them in one regression table in the layout of this tutorial
interpretations of the coefficients with units and reference categories
a t-test of one coefficient and an overall or partial F-test
\(R^2\), adjusted \(R^2\), and residual diagnostics
one graph of fitted values from the model
a conclusion of 150 words that clearly separates three things: the association, its uncertainty, and the reasons why it is not causal.







Check a model structure





A good solution could fit
m <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
or a model with a quadratic term for season and the group dummies. Keep season_c and women in the model next to their interaction (the hierarchy principle), and name the reference category. Interpret slopes that combine several coefficients, or differences between fitted values. Use anova() to compare the model with a nested reduced model. Inspect the residuals, including rstandard() and Cook’s distance, and plot fitted values inside Seasons 1–16. The conclusion must say that the team categories are broad, that only broadcast pitches are in the file, and that the results therefore do not show a causal effect of gender or season.





Check your understanding
Complete from memory:

A coefficient in a multiple regression compares cases that …
In a model with an intercept, R includes a factor with three categories as …
In the model season_c * women + ask_1k, the season slope for teams with women is …
Centring a predictor changes …, and it does not change …
In a model with \(x\) and \(x^2\), the fitted change from \(x\) to \(x+1\) is …







Check your answers






Differ in that predictor and have the same values of the other included predictors.
Two dummy variables. The third category is the reference category.
The coefficient of season_c plus the coefficient of season_c:women.
The meaning and the value of the intercept and of the coefficients that are read at \(x=0\). It does not change the fitted values or the interaction coefficient.
\(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)\).






Make it yours

Two sentences about your own venture
Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Describe in two sentences the full analysis that you would run on its data. First, name the outcome, two predictors, and one extension (a set of dummies, an interaction, or a quadratic term) that answers a real question. Second, say which limit you would mention first in your conclusion: selection, measurement, or omitted variables. There is no wrong answer.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus. “Outcome: weekly orders. Predictors: advertising spend and price, plus a dummy for exam weeks and its interaction with advertising spend, because I believe advertising works mainly when students are on campus. The first limit is omitted variables: the weather affects both how many flyers I hand out and how many people are on campus, and nothing in my data measures it.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant. Ask it to review your two sentences before you spend a lot of time on the data.



More practice
For extra exercises on the lectures of this tutorial, with worked solutions, ask Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant. For example: “Give me an extra exercise for Intermediate Tutorial 2. Show the solution only after I send my answer.”
This is the end of the QM Intermediate lectures and tutorials. Review the QM Intermediate Code Sheet, attempt the QM Intermediate Mock Exam, then return to the R Refresher, Mathematics Refresher, or the External Video Guide whenever you want to review a specific topic.
Continue to QM Intermediate Code Sheet.

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
text:
Lecture 1: Simple linear regression
Population model and fitted line
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\widehat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_i.
\]
OLS estimates in simple regression
\[
\hat\beta_1=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}
=\frac{s_{XY}}{s_X^2}
=r_{XY}\,\frac{s_Y}{s_X},
\qquad
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.
\]
Residual and sum of squared residuals
\[
e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2.
\]
Change of the units of measurement by a factor \(c\)



Multiplied by \(c\)
New intercept
New slope




outcome only
\(c\,\hat\beta_0\)
\(c\,\hat\beta_1\)


predictor only
\(\hat\beta_0\)
\(\hat\beta_1/c\)


outcome and predictor
\(c\,\hat\beta_0\)
\(\hat\beta_1\)



Fit a simple regression
m <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
coef(m)          # estimates
summary(m)       # coefficient table and fit
fitted(m)        # fitted values
residuals(m)     # residuals
Scatter plot with the fitted line
plot(y ~ x, data = dat,
     xlab = "Predictor (unit)", ylab = "Outcome (unit)")
abline(m, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
Fitted values for chosen values x_A and x_B of the predictor
b <- coef(m)
b[1] + b[2] * x_A                  # fitted value by hand

new_cases <- data.frame(x = c(x_A, x_B))

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
section: Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
text:
Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
Two-sided test of one coefficient
\[
H_0:\beta_j=0,
\qquad
H_1:\beta_j\ne0,
\qquad
t=\frac{\hat\beta_j}{\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)}.
\]
\[
\text{Reject }H_0\text{ at the 5\% level if }|t_{obs}|\ge t_{0.975,\,df}.
\]
Degrees of freedom and 95% confidence interval, model with \(k\) slopes and an intercept
\[
df=n-k-1,
\qquad
\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,\,df}\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j),
\qquad
\text{simple regression: }k=1,\ df=n-2.
\]
summary(m)                  # coefficient table and fit
confint(m, level = 0.95)    # 95% confidence intervals
df.residual(m)              # residual degrees of freedom
qt(0.975, df.residual(m))   # critical value, 95% interval
Labels in the output of summary(m)







Label in the output
Symbol




Estimate
\(\hat\beta_j\)


Std. Error
\(\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)\)


t value
\(t\)


Pr(>|t|)
two-sided p-value for \(H_0:\beta_j=0\)


Residual standard error
\(s\), with \(df=n-k-1\)


Multiple R-squared
\(R^2\)


Adjusted R-squared
\(R^2_{\text{adjusted}}\)


F-statistic
overall \(F\), with \(k\) and \(n-k-1\) degrees of freedom



The t statistic and the two-sided p-value step by step
tab <- summary(m)$coefficients
t_value <- tab["x", "Estimate"] / tab["x", "Std. Error"]
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = df.residual(m))
Sums of squares and \(R^2\)
\[
\text{SST}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2,\qquad
\text{SSE}=\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2,\qquad
\text{SSR}=\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2,
\]
\[
\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE},
\qquad
R^2=1-\frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}
=\frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}.
\]
y <- dat$y            # outcome values
yhat <- fitted(m)    # fitted values

SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
SSE <- sum(residuals(m)^2)
SSR <- SST - SSE
R2 <- 1 - SSE / SST
Residual standard error and adjusted \(R^2\)
\[
s=\sqrt{\frac{\text{SSE}}{n-k-1}},
\qquad
R^2_{\text{adjusted}}
=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-k-1}.
\]
summary(m)$r.squared        # R squared
summary(m)$fstatistic       # overall F, k, and n - k - 1
Overall F-test, model with \(k\) slopes
\[
H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=0,
\qquad
H_1:\text{at least one of }\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k\text{ is not }0,
\]
\[
F=\frac{\text{SSR}/k}{\text{SSE}/(n-k-1)},
\qquad
\text{simple regression: }F=t^2.
\]
Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (HC1)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# robust standard errors, t statistics, and p-values
coeftest(m, vcov. = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1"))
# robust 95% confidence intervals
coefci(m, vcov. = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1"))

Model with \(k\) predictors
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kX_{ik}+\varepsilon_i.
\]
m_multi <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = analysis)
summary(m_multi)     # coefficient table and fit
confint(m_multi)     # 95% confidence intervals
Fitted difference for changes \(\Delta x_1,\ldots,\Delta x_k\) of the predictors
\[
\Delta\widehat Y=\hat\beta_1\Delta x_1+\cdots+\hat\beta_k\Delta x_k.
\]
Fitted difference between two cases A and B
cases <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(x1_A, x1_B),
  x2 = c(x2_A, x2_B),
  x3 = c(x3_A, x3_B)
)
fits <- predict(m_multi, newdata = cases)  # fitted values
fits[2] - fits[1]                          # B minus A
Regression table with one column per model
# install once: install.packages("modelsummary")
library(modelsummary)
m_a <- lm(y ~ x1, data = analysis)
m_b <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = analysis)
modelsummary(
  list("(1)" = m_a, "(2)" = m_b, "(3)" = m_multi),
  stars = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared")
)

Lecture 5: Categories as predictors and joint tests
Reference category and model with a categorical predictor
analysis$group <- factor(analysis$group)
# categories: the first one is the reference
levels(analysis$group)

The same model with another reference category
analysis$group_alt <- relevel(analysis$group,

all.equal(fitted(m_group), fitted(m_alt))
Partial F-test of nested models
reduced <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = analysis)
complete <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + group, data = analysis)
anova(reduced, complete)

title: QM Intermediate Mock Exam
text:
How this mock exam works
This mock exam covers all six lectures of the course. It has 100 points, so your test score is
\[
\text{test score} = \frac{\text{points earned}}{10},
\]
on a scale from 1.00 to 10.00, with two decimals. A score below 1.00 counts as 1.00. The lecturer enters this test score in Osiris. Osiris then rounds it to a whole or half grade for your final course grade. A score from 5.50 to 5.74 becomes 6.0, and a score from 5.25 to 5.49 becomes 5.0. For example, 72 points give a test score of 7.20 and a final grade of 7.0. You pass with a final grade of 6.0 or higher, that is, with 55 points or more.
You take the Intermediate exam in TestVision. It lasts 120 minutes. You may use RStudio, Excel, the calculator in TestVision, a simple pocket calculator, and scrap paper. The practice exam in TestVision appears in your own TestVision account once the lecturer publishes it. You log in with your university account. There is no separate link. General information about TestVision for students is on the university page about TestVision.
You receive the QM Intermediate Code Sheet at the exam. Keep it open while you work on this mock exam.
Use 120 minutes as the practice time limit, as in the exam.
This mock exam gives an impression of what an exam in this course can look like. You download a data file, you run R yourself, and you type your answers.
All parts are open questions. You type a number with your calculation, or one to three sentences. An answer without a calculation or an explanation gets no points, unless the part asks only to report or to state something.
You do not have to simulate data, and you do not have to reproduce a simulation. The practice data are invented. The code that made them is in a collapsed box at the end of this page. It is there only so that anyone can check how we made the data. It is not part of the exam.
A part that starts with “In R:” needs code that you write and run yourself. Its answer is not printed in the question. For these parts, copy the R code that you used into your answer, and type the numbers that the part asks for. You can answer all other parts from your own results, from printed output, or with a short calculation. You may use R as a calculator everywhere.
Question 3 shows an R output of a colleague, and Question 4 shows a regression table in the layout of a research paper. You interpret them. Question 6 shows an answer of an AI assistant. You assess it.
All tests in this course are two-sided. Use a 5% significance level. Some parts that build on an “In R:” part print stand-in values. Use them if your code does not run.

title: QM Intermediate Mock Exam
text:
Dataset used throughout
The practice data are invented. Treat them as a simple random sample of 320 young ventures from a business registry. One row is one venture. The data are observational: none of the predictors was assigned by chance.

growth_pct: growth of annual sales compared with the year before, in percent. A value of 12 means that sales were 12% higher than in the year before
marketing_10k: annual marketing spending, in €10,000s. The values run from 0.25 (€2,500) to 7.99 (€79,900)
experience_years: prior industry experience of the lead founder, in years, from 0 to 18
team_size: number of current team members, from 1 to 10
digital: No for a mainly physical offering and Yes for a mainly digital offering. No is the reference category
spend_c: marketing_10k - 4, marketing spending centred at €40,000. This is close to the sample mean of about €40,400.

The population is the set of ventures in this registry. The data do not measure later survival or market conditions.
Download qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv, save it in the folder data of your R project, and load it with the code below. If you save the file directly in your project folder, write "qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv" as the file name.

ventures <- read.csv("data/qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv")
ventures$digital <- factor(ventures$digital, levels = c("No", "Yes"))

title: QM Intermediate Mock Exam
text:
Question 1: Simple regression (13 points)
A founder asks whether ventures that spend more on marketing grow faster. The outcome is growth_pct and the predictor is marketing_10k.

In R: load the data and check that the file has 320 rows. Report the mean and the largest value of growth_pct. (2 points)
In R: fit the simple regression of growth_pct on marketing_10k. Report the intercept and the slope. (2 points)
Stand-in values, if your code does not run: intercept 6.6 and slope 1.4. Use them in parts 3 and 4.
Interpret the slope in one sentence. (4 points)
In R: use predict() to calculate the fitted growth of a venture that spends €50,000 on marketing. The actual sales growth of this venture is 11%. Calculate its residual. State what the sign of the residual means. (5 points)







Model answer





Code

# Part 1
ventures <- read.csv("data/qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv")
ventures$digital <- factor(ventures$digital, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
nrow(ventures)

[1] 320

mean(ventures$growth_pct)

[1] 12.17166

max(ventures$growth_pct)

[1] 31.94

# Part 2
simple_model <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures)
coef(simple_model)

  (Intercept) marketing_10k 
     6.598158      1.378342 

# Part 4
fit_50k <- predict(simple_model, newdata = data.frame(marketing_10k = 5))
fit_50k

       1 
13.48987 

11 - fit_50k

        1 
-2.489868 


Answers

The file has 320 rows. The mean sales growth is 12.172%. The largest sales growth is 31.94%.
Intercept 6.598 and slope 1.378. The fitted line is \(\widehat{growth\_pct}=6.598+1.378\,marketing\_10k\).
Among the 320 sampled ventures, a venture that spends €10,000 more on marketing has on average 1.38 percentage points higher fitted sales growth.
€50,000 is marketing_10k = 5. The fitted growth is 13.49%. The residual is \(11-13.49=-2.49\) percentage points. The sign is negative: this venture grew less than the fitted growth for ventures with the same marketing spending.

title: QM Intermediate Mock Exam
text:
Question 2: Assumptions and diagnostics (15 points)
Check the model of Question 1, growth_pct ~ marketing_10k. Parts 1 and 4 ask for two plots.

In R: make the residual-versus-fitted plot of the model. Describe in one sentence the pattern that you see. State the assumption that this pattern challenges. (5 points)
In R: count the ventures with a standardised residual beyond \(\pm3\). Then count the ventures with a Cook’s distance above \(4/n\). Report both counts. (2 points)
A colleague wants to delete all ventures that part 2 flags, “to get a cleaner model”. Respond to her plan in two or three sentences. State the rule of Lecture 2 for flagged observations, and say what you would do with these ventures. (4 points)
In R: make the normal Q–Q plot of the standardised residuals. Describe in one sentence how the points lie relative to the line. Then explain in one sentence whether a departure from normality is a serious problem for this model with 320 ventures. (4 points)







Model answer





Code

# Part 1
plot(fitted(simple_model), residuals(simple_model),
     xlab = "Fitted value", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)









# Part 2
sum(abs(rstandard(simple_model)) > 3)

[1] 1

sum(cooks.distance(simple_model) > 4 / nobs(simple_model))

[1] 19



# Part 4
qqnorm(rstandard(simple_model))
qqline(rstandard(simple_model))








Answers

The vertical spread of the residuals grows from left to right, that is, with the fitted growth. The points form a fan shape. This is heteroskedasticity, so it challenges the assumption of homoskedasticity (constant variance of the errors).
One venture has a standardised residual beyond \(\pm3\). 19 ventures have a Cook’s distance above \(4/n=4/320=0.0125\).
The rule is: investigate, report, never silently delete. Investigate means to look at the flagged ventures in the data and to ask whether a value is an error or whether the venture is of a different kind. Report means to fit the model with and without these ventures, to show both results, and to say which one you use and why.
The points follow the line in the middle. At the upper end they lie above the line, and near the lower end slightly below it. This is not a serious problem here. Normal errors matter in small samples. With 320 ventures the tests and intervals still hold approximately.

title: QM Intermediate Mock Exam
text:
Question 3: Inference and fit (10 points)
A colleague drew 200 of the 320 ventures at random and fitted the model below to these 200 ventures. You do not know which ventures she drew, so you cannot run this model yourself. Answer from her output. The formulas are on the code sheet.
Call:
lm(formula = growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + 
    digital, data = ventures_200)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-11.2970  -2.7338  -0.0992   2.6132  12.3786 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       2.73159    0.78897   3.462 0.000658 ***
marketing_10k     1.35473    0.12868  10.528  < 2e-16 ***
experience_years  0.28585    0.05277   5.417 1.77e-07 ***
digitalYes        3.17544    0.58246   5.452 1.49e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.049 on 196 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4803,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4723 
F-statistic: 60.38 on 3 and 196 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
For this model, SSE = 3212.85 and SST = 6181.93. The critical value for a 95% confidence interval and a 5% test with 196 degrees of freedom is \(t_{0.975,\,196}=1.972\). In R, qt(0.975, 196) gives it.

(a) Show with a calculation how the Multiple R-squared follows from SSE and SST. (b) State in one sentence what this number says about the model for these 200 ventures. (4 points)
(a) Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the coefficient of marketing_10k. Write the five parts of the exam procedure of Lecture 3. (b) State whether the 5% test rejects a coefficient of zero, and explain how the interval shows this. (6 points)







Model answer





Answers

(a) \(R^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}=1-3212.85/6181.93=0.48\). (b) Among these 200 ventures, the model explains about 48% of the variation in sales growth.
(a) The five parts of the interval:

Formula. \(\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,\,df}\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)\), with \(df=n-k-1=200-3-1=196\).
Given values. \(\hat\beta_j=1.35473\), \(\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)=0.12868\), and \(t_{0.975,\,196}=1.972\).
Calculations. The margin of error is \(1.972\times0.12868=0.254\).
Interval. \((1.355-0.254,\ 1.355+0.254)=(1.10,\ 1.61)\) percentage points per €10,000.
Conclusion. See (b).

(b) Zero lies outside the interval. The interval contains the values of the coefficient that the two-sided 5% test does not reject, so the test rejects a coefficient of zero. At the 5% level we can conclude the following for all ventures in the registry: at the same experience and offering type, more marketing spending goes with higher sales growth.

The critical value for a 95% confidence interval and a 5% test is \(t_{0.975,\,df}=1.967\) in all three columns. For column (3), with \(df=320-4-1=315\), R gives it with qt(0.975, 315).

Team size has no star in column (3). Calculate its t statistic. Then state what the missing star means and what it does not mean. (4 points)
Venture B spends €30,000 more on marketing than venture A. Its lead founder has 4 more years of experience. B has a digital offering and A a physical one. Both have the same team size. Calculate the fitted growth of B minus the fitted growth of A with column (3). (5 points)
Founder experience has three stars in column (2). Still, adding it moves the marketing coefficient only from 1.340 to 1.338. Explain in one or two sentences what this says about experience and marketing spending in this sample. Then state one problem that the stable coefficient does not exclude. (5 points)
In R: test whether founder experience and team size together improve the model of column (1). Fit the models of columns (1) and (3) and compare them with anova(). Report the F statistic. Then show how F follows from the two residual sums of squares in your output. (4 points)
Stand-in values, if your code does not run: the residual sum of squares is about 5950 on 317 degrees of freedom for column (1). It is about 5270 on 315 degrees of freedom for column (3). Calculate F from them. For part 5, use a p-value below 0.001.
State the null hypothesis of the test in part 4 and your conclusion at the 5% level. Then explain in one sentence how this conclusion and the missing star of team size can both be true. (5 points)







Model answer





Code

# Part 4
col_1 <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + digital, data = ventures)
col_3 <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + digital + experience_years + team_size,
  data = ventures
)
anova(col_1, col_3)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + digital
Model 2: growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + digital + experience_years + team_size
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    317 5949.3                                  
2    315 5272.6  2    676.77 20.216 5.491e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Answers

\(t=0.168/0.103=1.63\). The test in five steps:

Hypotheses. \(H_0:\beta_{team}=0\) versus \(H_1:\beta_{team}\ne0\), where \(\beta_{team}\) is the coefficient of team size in the model of column (3) for all ventures of the registry. The significance level is \(\alpha=0.05\).
Test statistic. \(T=\hat\beta_{team}/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_{team})\), which has the \(t_{315}\) distribution if \(H_0\) is true.
Critical value and rejection region. \(t_{0.975,\,315}=1.967\). Reject \(H_0\) if \(t\le-1.967\) or \(t\ge1.967\).
Observed value. The numbers in parentheses are standard errors, so \(t=0.168/0.103=1.63\).
Conclusion. 1.63 lies between \(-1.967\) and 1.967, so do not reject \(H_0\). The p-value is above 0.05, and so there is no star. At the 5% level we cannot conclude that team size goes with growth at fixed marketing spending, offering type, and experience.

What the missing star does not mean: it does not show that the coefficient is zero. The 95% interval, \(0.168\pm1.967\times0.103\), runs from \(-0.035\) to 0.371 percentage points per team member. It contains zero and also clearly positive values.
Marketing: €30,000 is 3 steps, so \(3\times1.341=4.023\). Experience: \(4\times0.258=1.032\). Digital offering: 3.084. Sum: \(4.023+1.032+3.084=8.14\) percentage points.
A coefficient changes when the added predictor is related to the outcome and also to the predictor of interest. Experience is related to growth, but in this sample it is almost unrelated to marketing spending. So holding it fixed changes the marketing comparison very little. The stable coefficient does not exclude a variable that is not in the data and that is related to both marketing spending and growth, for example the quality of the product.
\(F=20.216\). From the output, with the partial F statistic, \(q=2\), and \(df=315\): \(F=\dfrac{(5949.3-5272.6)/2}{5272.6/315}=\dfrac{338.35}{16.74}=20.21\).
\(H_0\): the coefficients of founder experience and team size are both zero. The p-value in the anova() output is 5.491e-09, that is 0.000000005, far below 0.05. So reject \(H_0\). At the 5% level we can conclude that the two predictors together improve the model of column (1). The F-test asks about the two terms together, and the t-test asks about team size alone. The joint result comes from experience. A set of terms can be jointly significant while one of its terms is not significant.

marketing_10k 2.179 and I(marketing_10k^2) \(-0.105\).
The fitted change from \(x\) to \(x+1\) is \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)\). From €20,000 to €30,000, \(x=2\): \(2.1794-0.1046\times5=1.66\) percentage points. From €60,000 to €70,000, \(x=6\): \(2.1794-0.1046\times13=0.82\) percentage points. Together: the same extra €10,000 goes with about half as much extra growth at the higher level of spending. The fitted curve becomes flatter.
€150,000 is far outside the range of the data. The largest spending in the sample is €79,900. No venture in the data supports the curve there. A quadratic curve does not stop curving. This one turns downward at about €104,000 of spending, and no data show such a turn.

title: QM Intermediate Mock Exam
section: Question 6: An answer of an AI assistant, and a decision (20 points)
text:
Question 6: An answer of an AI assistant, and a decision (20 points)
Sara runs a young venture with a mainly digital offering. She gave column (3) of the table in Question 4 to an AI assistant. Here is column (3) again:
Outcome: sales growth (%), 320 ventures     Estimate  Std. Error
Marketing spending (€10,000s)                  1.341       0.100
Digital offering (1 = yes)                     3.084       0.463
Founder experience (years)                     0.258       0.041
Team size (members)                            0.168       0.103
Intercept                                      2.449       0.771
She asked: “What does this mean for my marketing budget?” The AI answered:

“Good news. Your model controls for experience, team size, and offering type. So the marketing coefficient is a causal effect: if you spend €20,000 more on marketing, your sales growth will rise by 2.68 percentage points. Your venture is digital, and digital ventures grow 3.084% faster than the average venture. And the p-value of marketing is below 0.001, which proves that the assumptions of the model hold.”


Assess the claim that the marketing coefficient is a causal effect. (a) Explain whether the control variables in the model justify this claim. (b) Write a sentence about €20,000 more marketing spending that the table does support. (5 points)
Assess the sentence about digital ventures. Explain two errors in it, and write a correct sentence about the coefficient 3.084. (4 points)
Assess the last sentence. (a) Explain whether a small p-value can show that the assumptions of the model hold. (b) State what the small p-value of marketing does show. (4 points)

Sara’s venture had sales of €1,000,000 last year. So 1 percentage point of sales growth is €10,000 of extra sales. Of each euro of sales, 50 cents are left as margin after the direct costs. Sara is considering spending €10,000 more on marketing next year.

The 95% confidence interval of the marketing coefficient in column (3) runs from 1.14 to 1.54 percentage points per €10,000. Show with a calculation that €10,000 more marketing spending goes with extra sales between €11,400 and €15,400, and with an extra margin between €5,700 and €7,700. (2 points)
(a) Decide whether Sara should spend the extra €10,000 on the basis of these numbers, and give your reason in one sentence. (b) Explain one reason why her true gain could differ from these numbers. (5 points)







Model answer





Answers

(a) No. A control variable holds fixed only what is measured and in the model. Variables that are not in the data can influence both marketing spending and growth, for example the quality of the product. (b) “At the same experience, team size, and offering type, ventures that spend €20,000 more on marketing have on average 2.68 percentage points higher fitted sales growth.”
The outcome is in percent, so the difference is 3.084 percentage points, not 3.084%: “3.084% faster” would be a relative change. The comparison is with the reference category, ventures with a mainly physical offering, and not with the average venture. A correct sentence: “Ventures with a mainly digital offering have on average 3.084 percentage points higher fitted sales growth than ventures with a mainly physical offering that have the same marketing spending, experience, and team size.”
(a) No. A p-value is calculated under the assumptions of the model, so it cannot prove them. (b) The small p-value is evidence against a marketing coefficient of zero, if the assumptions hold.
Extra sales: \(1.14\times\text{€}10{,}000=\text{€}11{,}400\) at the lower end and \(1.54\times\text{€}10{,}000=\text{€}15{,}400\) at the upper end. Extra margin at 50 cents per euro: \(0.5\times\text{€}11{,}400=\text{€}5{,}700\) and \(0.5\times\text{€}15{,}400=\text{€}7{,}700\).
(a) Decision: do not spend the extra €10,000 on this evidence. Reason: even at the upper end of the interval, the extra margin of €7,700 is below the €10,000 that the marketing costs.
(b) The coefficient is an association among 320 ventures in observational data. It is not the effect of a change in her own budget, which can be smaller or larger.




The questions of this mock exam have 100 points together. Do the mock exam in R before you open the answers. Use the model answers to check your numbers, and also your units, reference categories, statements about what is held fixed, and the limits of causal claims.






Optional: how the practice data were made (not part of the exam)





You do not need this box for any question. The practice data were made with the code below. The fixed seed makes sure that the code always gives the same 320 rows as the file that you download. Answer every question for the registry data as the text describes them, not for this code.

set.seed(734)
n_mock <- 320
marketing_10k <- round(runif(n_mock, 0.25, 8), 2)
experience_years <- sample(0:18, n_mock, replace = TRUE)
team_size <- sample(
  1:10, n_mock, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(8, 16, 20, 20, 14, 9, 6, 4, 2, 1)
)
digital <- factor(
  ifelse(runif(n_mock) < 0.45, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("No", "Yes")
)
spend_c <- marketing_10k - 4
growth_mean <-
  8 + 1.10 * spend_c + 3 * (digital == "Yes") -
  0.10 * spend_c^2 + 0.30 * experience_years +
  0.70 * spend_c * (digital == "Yes") + 0.20 * team_size
growth_pct <- round(
  growth_mean + rnorm(n_mock, 0, 2.5 + 0.40 * marketing_10k),
  2
)
ventures <- data.frame(
  growth_pct, marketing_10k, experience_years, team_size, digital, spend_c
)

title: QM Advanced: Course overview
text:
QM Advanced builds on QM Intermediate. It combines statistical modelling with research design and prepares you for the quantitative thesis. The course takes place in the fourth semester and ends with a written exam. Its chapters are not online yet.
Continue to How to succeed in this course.

title: How to succeed in this course
text:
What is examined
Success in QM is not about talent for mathematics. It is about a short weekly routine that you repeat: prepare before class, take part in class, read and practise after class, and bring your attempts to the tutorial. Every lecture chapter follows this routine.
Why this routine works:
Practice spread over the weeks works better than the same amount of work packed together before the exam.
The lecture material and the tutorials are the exam material. Grey Optional boxes are not exam material. They contain formal versions, derivations, and extra topics for students who are interested.

In the lecture
In the lecture you often try a question with your neighbour before the answer is shown. Try it seriously, even when the question looks hard. A wrong attempt helps you learn. In QM Intermediate, bring your laptop. The code of the lecture is in the chapter, ready to copy. You can run each step yourself and get the same numbers and figures.

Exams. Both courses end with one exam that counts for 100% of the grade. All exam questions are open questions. Each exam has 100 points. Your test score is the number of points divided by 10, with two decimals and a minimum of 1.00. section: Working with AI, in one paragraph
text:
Working with AI, in one paragraph
Use the Tilly bot of your course (linked on the course overview page) and other AI tools with the protocol Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain. Attempt the task yourself first and find where you are stuck. Ask for a hint or for a question that helps you find your mistake, not for a full solution. Verify every answer against the data, the course notation, and the R output. Then explain the result in your own words. What counts in this course is what you can do yourself with data and output. With this protocol, AI improves this skill instead of replacing it.
