title: R Refresher
text:
If regression commands are unfamiliar
Use the same workflow throughout QM Intermediate. First store the fitted model as an object, then inspect it:
model <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = my_data)
summary(model)
confint(model)
fitted(model)
residuals(model)
plot(model)

lm() fits the model. The predictors are to the right of ~, and the outcome is on the left.
summary() reports the coefficients, their usual t-tests, the model fit, and the overall F-test.
confint() reports confidence intervals for the coefficients.
fitted() and residuals() return one value for each row of the analysis sample.
plot(model) opens the standard diagnostic plots.

Give the fitted object a meaningful name. Inspect the analysis sample before you interpret the output. If a variable in the model has a missing value in a row, lm() leaves out that row without a warning, unless you tell it to do something else. The Intermediate code sheet lists the R commands of the course in one place.

title: R Refresher
text:
A quick return-to-R check
Run this code yourself, without copying the answers from someone else:
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv")
nrow(sharks)
mean(sharks$deal_on_show)
median(sharks$description_words)
table(sharks$season)
Then explain each output in words. If the code runs but you cannot explain a number, your problem is with the statistics, not with the programming.






Assessment reminder



QM Basic ends with a written exam, and its lectures and tutorials ask you to read and interpret R code and output. The QM Intermediate exam is in TestVision, and R is available during the exam. QM Advanced also ends with a written exam. So this refresher matters most for QM Intermediate.

title: R Refresher
text:
Making figures in R
Every data figure in this textbook comes with its R code. Click “See the R code for this figure” above a graph to open the code. You can copy the code into a fresh R session in your course project, and it draws the same figure. You do not need to write ggplot2 code yourself in this course. The base R commands on the code sheet are enough. To run the code of this book on your own laptop, you need four packages. Install them once:
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "lmtest", "sandwich", "modelsummary"))
Some rules for the graphs in your own tutorials, reports, and thesis:

One message per graph. State it in the caption. Remove everything that does not support this message (boxes, minor gridlines, decoration).
Counts start at zero, and a graph has only one vertical axis.
Use few colours. Take one colour for the data (#009E73), a second for a contrast or a fitted line (#D55E00), and grey for context. Draw reference values (means, benchmarks, zero lines) as dashed lines and write the value next to them. Colour-blind readers can tell these two data colours apart.
Put labels directly on the graph where possible in place of a legend, and always name the axes with their units.
Choose the form that fits. Draw a PMF as sticks with dots, a histogram with a stated bin width, and a model curve as a smooth line.

Three free references go further, and they are useful for your thesis. Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund, R for Data Science, Chapter 1, explains ggplot2 itself. Healy, Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction, shows how to build good graphs in R from start to end. Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization, explains the design principles.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Numbers, proportions, percentages, and units
A proportion is a part divided by a total:
\[
\text{proportion}=\frac{\text{count in category}}{\text{total count}}.
\]
Convert a proportion to a percentage by multiplying by 100. A change from 40% to 46% is:

a 6 percentage-point increase
a \(6/40=15\%\) relative increase.

Keep the units in every calculation. If \(Y\) is the equity offered in percent and \(X\) is measured in seasons, a slope has units of percentage points per season. If you change the unit from dollars to thousands of dollars, the size of the coefficient changes, but the fitted relationship stays the same.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Order of operations
Use this order:

brackets or parentheses
powers and roots
multiplication and division
addition and subtraction.

For example,
\[
\frac{12-8}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{4}{4}=1.
\]
In R:
(12 - 8) / sqrt(16)
In code, use plenty of parentheses when they make the calculation clearer.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Equality, approximation, and inequalities



Symbol
Read as




\(=\)
equals


\(\ne\)
does not equal


\(\approx\)
is approximately equal to


\(<,>\)
is less than, is greater than


\(\le,\ge\)
is less/greater than or equal to


\(\in\)
is an element of



Do not write \(\approx\) when a value is exact. For example, rounded R output may show a probability of approximately 0.612, but the fraction \(882/1441\) is the exact value for the file.
Interval notation:

\([a,b]\) includes both endpoints
\((a,b)\) excludes both endpoints
\((a,b]\) excludes \(a\) and includes \(b\).

For a continuous random variable, it does not matter for a probability whether an interval includes its endpoints. The reason is that single points have probability zero.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Variables, functions, and graphs
A variable is a symbol whose value can change. A function assigns one output to each allowed input:
\[
y=f(x).
\]
In \(F_X(x)=P(X\le x)\), \(F_X\) is the name of the CDF, and \(x\) is the input value at which we evaluate it. The subscript shows which random variable the CDF describes.
The horizontal axis of a graph shows the input or predictor. The vertical axis shows the function value or outcome. Read both labels and units before you interpret the shape of the graph.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Straight lines, slopes, and intercepts
A line is
\[
y=a+bx.
\]

\(a\) is the value of \(y\) at \(x=0\): the intercept.
\(b\) is the change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x\): the slope.

Between two points \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\),
\[
b=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.
\]
The sign gives the direction. The size of the slope depends on the units of both variables. When \(x=0\) is outside the observed range, the intercept may have no useful meaning.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Subscripts and indices
The symbol \(x_i\) means the value of variable \(x\) for observation \(i\). For \(n\) observations,
\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n.
\]
In multiple regression, \(x_{ij}\) is the value of predictor \(j\) for observation \(i\). Keep the two roles separate:

\(i=1,\ldots,n\) numbers the observations
\(j=1,\ldots,k\) numbers the predictors.

Capital \(X_i\) usually stands for a random variable before sampling. Lower-case \(x_i\) stands for its observed value.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Summation notation
The Greek letter sigma means “add up”:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n.
\]
The sample mean is
\[
\bar x=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.
\]
For values 2, 5, and 8,
\[
\bar x=\frac{2+5+8}{3}=5.
\]
A weighted sum multiplies every value by its weight and then adds the results. The expected value of a discrete random variable is a weighted sum with the probabilities as weights:
\[
E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x).
\]

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Powers, roots, and squared deviations
The square is \(x^2=x\times x\). The square root undoes the square of a non-negative number. In general:
\[
\sqrt{x^2}=|x|.
\]
Squaring a deviation makes both signs positive and gives large deviations more weight. This is why variance (Basic Lecture 3) and least squares use squared terms.
The variance is in squared units. Its square root, the standard deviation, is in the original units again.
The square-root rule holds for the standard deviation of the sample mean, \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=\sigma/\sqrt n\), and for the standard error, \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=S/\sqrt n\), with the value \(s/\sqrt n\) in one sample. To halve either, multiply \(n\) by \(2^2=4\).

title: Mathematics Refresher
section: Degrees of freedom and t critical values
text:
Degrees of freedom and t critical values
Degrees of freedom count how many pieces of information are still free after you estimate the quantities that the procedure needs. For a one-sample t procedure, the \(n\) deviations from the sample mean always add up to zero:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)=0.
\]
If you know \(n-1\) of the deviations, this condition fixes the last one. So the procedure uses
\[
df=n-1.
\]
The notation \(t_{0.975,\,df}\) means the value with 97.5% of a t distribution to its left. It leaves 2.5% in the right tail, so \(\pm t_{0.975,\,df}\) are the critical values for a 95% two-sided procedure. In R:
qt(0.975, df = 24)
With few degrees of freedom, the t distribution has more probability in its tails, and the critical value is larger. As the degrees of freedom increase, the t distribution comes closer to the standard normal distribution.
The same idea appears again in regression. If a model estimates an intercept and \(k\) slopes from \(n\) observations, the residual degrees of freedom are
\[
df=n-k-1.
\]

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Sets and event notation
A set is a collection of elements. In probability:

\(\Omega\) is the sample space
\(A\subseteq\Omega\) is an event
\(A^c\) is the complement, “not \(A\)”
\(A\cup B\) is the union, “\(A\) or \(B\), or both”
\(A\cap B\) is the intersection, “both \(A\) and \(B\)”
\(\varnothing\) is the empty event.

In conditional probability,
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},
\]
the vertical bar means “given”. The event after the bar defines the group that you look at, and its probability is the denominator.
Two events are independent when \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\), or equivalently when \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)\). Basic Lecture 4 checks both forms.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Fractions and rearranging equations
Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number does not change a fraction. To solve a simple equation, apply the same operation to both sides.
Example:
\[
z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}
\]
implies
\[
z\sigma=x-\mu
\]
and therefore
\[
x=\mu+z\sigma.
\]
With this rearrangement you can go from a z-score to a raw value and back.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Standardisation and z-scores
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean:
\[
z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}.
\]
An invented example. The monthly sales of a shop have mean \(\mu=200\) units and standard deviation \(\sigma=40\) units. A month with sales of 260 units has \(z=(260-200)/40=1.5\). It lies 1.5 standard deviations above the mean. A negative z-score means a value below the mean. To go back from \(z\) to \(x\), use \(x=\mu+z\sigma\) from the previous section.
The same form appears in the tests of Basic Lecture 10 and in regression output: an estimate minus a claimed value, divided by its standard deviation or its standard error.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Indicators and reference categories
An indicator is also called a dummy variable. It takes only the values 0 and 1:
\[
D_i=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{condition holds},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
In \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1D+\varepsilon\):

\(D=0\) gives mean \(\beta_0\)
\(D=1\) gives mean \(\beta_0+\beta_1\)
\(\beta_1\) is the mean of the group with \(D=1\) minus the mean of the group with \(D=0\).

For \(G\) categories and an intercept, use \(G-1\) indicators. Name the reference category, which has no indicator.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Products, interactions, and combined effects
An interaction contains a product \(XZ\):
\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2Z+\beta_3XZ+\varepsilon.
\]
The slope of \(X\) is \(\beta_1+\beta_3Z\). When \(Z=0\), it is \(\beta_1\). When \(Z=1\), it is \(\beta_1+\beta_3\). Interpret the combined expression, not \(\beta_3\) alone.
Centring replaces \(X\) with
\[
X_c=X-\bar X.
\]
Then \(X_c=0\) stands for the sample mean of \(X\). This often gives the coefficients of the terms without the product a more useful meaning. Centring changes some coefficients and their meaning, but it does not change the fitted values of the model.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Polynomial terms
A quadratic function is
\[
y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2.
\]
The change from \(x\) to \(x+1\) is
\[
\beta_1+\beta_2(2x+1),
\]
so there is no single constant slope. Calculate fitted values at useful values of \(x\), and graph the curve only within the observed range.
In an R formula, write a squared predictor as I(x^2) so that R calculates the square.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
References and further practice

OpenStax, College Algebra 2e has free chapters on equations, functions, graphs, polynomials, and algebraic manipulation.
Khan Academy Algebra has short explanations and practice on linear equations, functions, exponents, and polynomials.
R as a Calculator connects arithmetic and order of operations directly to R.

When you practise with AI, ask for one problem at a time and show your working. Ask for feedback on your first wrong step, not for a new full answer.
Continue to the External Video Guide.

title: External Video Guide
text:
Required preparation at a glance
The videos are an extra tool. They explain the key ideas of the course in another way, and they can use a different notation. Where a video and the lecture material differ, the lecture material and its notation come first.
This page lists the external videos that the course uses. Every clip has one of three purposes:
Only clips labelled Required before class are compulsory preparation. Review and extension clips add no exam material. If a video differs from this textbook in scope or notation, follow the textbook. QM Basic mainly uses MIT OpenCourseWare pages, which include videos and transcripts. QM Intermediate uses Stanford’s Statistical Learning series. The complete collections are the MIT probability playlist and the Stanford Statistical Learning playlist.

text:
Supplementary probability reading
MIT OpenCourseWare offers Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis’s Introduction to Probability: Selected Textbook Summary Material. The official page includes the PDF download. This 77-page text is a reference, not required reading. Read only a section that a lecture asks you to read, or that you need for review.

title: External Video Guide
section: Basic Lecture 2: Probability foundations and random variables
text:
Basic Lecture 2: Probability foundations and random variables
Required before class

01.2 Sample Space: outcomes, sample spaces, and events.
01.4 Probability Axioms: non-negativity, normalisation, and additivity.
05.2 Definition of Random Variables: a random variable as a function from outcomes to numbers.

Review when needed

01.3 Sample Space Examples: more examples of outcomes and events.
01.5 Simple Properties of Probabilities: complement and addition rules derived from the axioms.
01.10 Interpretations and Uses of Probabilities: how the meaning of a probability depends on the model.

Optional extension

01.7 A Discrete Example: a worked discrete probability model.

title: External Video Guide
section: Basic Lecture 3: Discrete distributions, expectation, and variance
text:
Basic Lecture 3: Discrete distributions, expectation, and variance
Required before class

05.3 Probability Mass Functions: point probabilities and the normalisation rule.
05.8 Expectation: expectation as a probability-weighted average.

Review when needed

05.4 Bernoulli and Indicator Random Variables: coding an event as 1 and its complement as 0.
06.2 Variance: expected squared distance from the mean. This lecture teaches variance and the standard deviation.

title: External Video Guide
section: Basic Lecture 4: Conditioning, Bayes’ rule, and independence
text:
Basic Lecture 4: Conditioning, Bayes’ rule, and independence
Required before class

02.2 Conditional Probabilities: limiting attention to the outcomes in the condition and rescaling their probabilities.
02.8 Bayes’ Rule: reversing a condition using base rates and likelihoods.

Review when needed

02.6 The Multiplication Rule: writing a joint probability with a conditional probability.
02.7 Total Probability Theorem: combining conditional probabilities across a partition (groups that do not overlap and together cover all outcomes).
03.3 Independence of Two Events: the conditional and product definitions of event independence, which this lecture covers.

Optional extension

02.3 A Die Roll Example: a worked conditioning example.

title: External Video Guide

text:
Basic Lecture 5: Joint random variables, covariance, and correlation
Required before class

06.7 Joint PMFs and the Expected Value Rule: joint probabilities and expectations involving two variables.
12.5 Covariance: covariance as an expected product of deviations.
12.8 The Correlation Coefficient: standardising covariance.

Review when needed

07.2 Conditional PMFs: the distribution of one variable at a fixed value of another variable.
07.4 Independence of Random Variables: checking whether every joint probability equals the product of the two corresponding marginal probabilities.
12.10 Interpreting the Correlation Coefficient: what correlation does and does not describe.

Optional extension

12.6 Covariance Properties: additional algebraic properties of covariance.
